docs.title: More than notation - From Monologue to Dialogue
docs.text:
The Saber Standard is not just a way to write attacks. It is a public, maintained choreography standard for documenting full saber movement: attacks, parries, body movement, transitions, spins and other actions.

It is written for both Saberists at once. Most notation record only the attacker's moves leading to a run of attacks answered in turn. One person acting and the other reacting from start to finish. That is a monologue, and on the floor it looks staged.

Every Saber Standard movement is written as two rows of equal standing: each Saberist has their own line, and either may attack or defend at any step. The initiative passes back and forth the way it does in a real exchange. That is what makes this a dialogue — a language two people speak, rather than a list of targets one person delivers.

docs.title: Relationship to SaberCraft
docs.text:
SaberCraft is the founding school and original community where the Saber Standard was developed. SaberCraft remains committed to community classes, community events, and training culture.

SaberCraft's CM library represents one implementation of the Saber Standard, but the notation system is designed to support choreography from other schools and communities as well.

Originated, developed and maintained by the SaberCraft community.

docs.title: Community growth without losing clarity
docs.text:
The Saber Standard is designed to support both:

  • stable official standards
  • community creativity and experimentation

This means schools, instructors, choreographers, and performance groups are encouraged to create original movement libraries using Saber Standard Notation.

At the same time, not every contribution automatically becomes official baseline material.

This page explains the current contribution philosophy.

Schools can publish choreography written in Saber Standard Notation while still maintaining their own identity.

The choreography does not become "owned" by the standard simply because it uses the notation language.

docs.text:

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text: This page answers common questions from students, schools, theater teachers, clubs, and choreographers who are new to the Saber Standard.

docs.title: Is the Saber Standard only for SaberCraft?
docs.text:
No. SaberCraft is the founding school, but the Saber Standard is designed for any group that wants to document choreographed saber movement clearly.

A school can use the Saber Standard without becoming SaberCraft.

docs.title: Do we have to use SaberCraft’s choreography?
docs.text:
No. SaberCraft has its own Core Movement library, but the Saber Standard is a notation standard, not a franchise.

Your school can create its own forms, drills, scenes, or choreography and write them using Saber Standard Notation.

docs.title: Is the Saber Standard only for Star Wars-inspired choreography?
docs.text:
No. The Saber Standard grew from saber choreography, but it also connects to theater, stage combat, martial arts-inspired movement, martial sports, and performance training.

The goal is clear movement documentation, not imitation of one franchise.

docs.title: What problem does the Saber Standard solve?
docs.text:
Most choreography is passed down through memory, video, and repeated in-person teaching.

That works until someone forgets a detail, changes the timing, leaves the group, or teaches it differently.

The Saber Standard gives groups a way to write choreography down so it can be taught, reviewed, preserved, and shared more consistently.

docs.title: Is the Saber Standard just attack notation?
docs.text:
No. Some notation systems mainly describe where an attack goes.

The Saber Standard is designed to describe the larger choreographic exchange.

It can include attacks, parries, defensive movement, turns, spins, ducks, jumps, recoils, locks, holds, thrusts, kicks, flourishes, transitions, and timing between performers.

Attack notation tells you where the saber goes. The Saber Standard is built to show what the whole choreography does.

docs.title: What is the difference between notation and a standard?
docs.text:
A notation system helps people write movement down.

A standard gives the community a public reference, shared definitions, version history, and a way to review whether choreography is being written clearly.

docs.title: Is the Saber Standard publicly available?
docs.text:
Yes. The notation material has been available online for over a decade, and this site is being built as the long-term public reference for the Saber Standard.

The goal is for students, teachers, schools, and clubs to have access to the same reference instead of relying on unavailable material or private interpretation.

docs.title: Is the Saber Standard free to use?
docs.text:
The public documentation is intended to be readable and usable by schools, clubs, instructors, and choreographers.

For specific reuse, publishing, or redistribution questions, see the Licensing page.

docs.title: Can a theater teacher use the Saber Standard for a stage fight?
docs.text:
Yes. The Saber Standard can help theater teachers and student performers document a fight scene so it can be rehearsed safely and repeated consistently.

It does not replace live instruction, fight direction, or safety judgment. It gives the team a written reference for the choreography.

docs.title: Can a high school or college club use the Saber Standard?
docs.text:
Yes. A club can start with the beginner path, learn the six beginner target lines, practice CM-A, and then begin writing short original exchanges.

Start here: Start Here / Beginner Path

docs.title: Can my school create its own choreography library?
docs.text:
Yes. That is part of the point.

Your school might create its own forms, scenes, drills, or performance sets and write them using the Saber Standard.

The shared notation makes choreography easier to read across groups, but each group can keep its own style and identity.

docs.title: How does choreography review work?
docs.text:
Formal review is part of the long-term vision.

A future Saber Standard review council or working group may help evaluate submitted choreography for clarity, safety, notation accuracy, and whether it belongs in the official core library, an extended library, or a community archive.

docs.title: Who maintains the Saber Standard?
docs.text:
The Saber Standard is currently maintained by Lumina Federation LLC and developed from the SaberCraft teaching community.

The standard is being organized publicly so questions, corrections, and future improvements can be handled in a more transparent way.

docs.title: How do I ask questions?
docs.text:
Use the official website and public community spaces connected to the Saber Standard and SaberCraft.

The goal is for questions to be answerable publicly whenever possible, so other schools and students can benefit from the same clarification.

docs.title: Keep your choreography. Share the language.
docs.text:
The Saber Standard is a shared notation standard for choreographed saber movement.

It was created so schools, performance groups, clubs, instructors, and independent choreographers can document and exchange choreography using a common movement language — without giving up their own identity, curriculum, or creative style.

You do not need to replace your school.

You do not need to adopt SaberCraft’s entire Core Movement library.

You do not need to teach the same choreography as anyone else.

Instead, the Saber Standard gives your group a way to:

  • write choreography clearly
  • preserve movement over time
  • teach more consistently
  • share sequences between instructors
  • archive choreography in a readable format
  • collaborate across schools and communities
  • reduce dependence on memory and video alone

docs.title: Why this is a standard, not just notation
docs.text:
A notation system helps people write movement down.

A standard gives people a public reference they can use, question, review, and build from over time.

That distinction matters for schools. If a movement language is hard to access, unavailable, or dependent on one person’s memory, different groups eventually create their own house rules. The Saber Standard is designed to avoid that by making the reference public, maintained, and reviewable.

docs.title: What the Saber Standard actually standardizes
docs.text:
The Saber Standard standardizes the language of choreography.

This includes:

  • target zones
  • attack notation
  • parry notation
  • body movement
  • defensive movement
  • flourishes
  • timing structure
  • table formatting
  • movement terminology
  • notation grammar

The standard does not require every group to use the same choreography library.

docs.title: Your choreography library remains yours
docs.text:
SaberCraft uses the Saber Standard to teach its own choreography library, including CM-A through CM-X.

Another school might create:

  • Academy Forms
  • Temple Drills
  • Stage Combat Exchanges
  • Tournament Sequences
  • Film Performance Sets
  • Original choreography collections

All of these can be written using the same notation language.

That means schools can exchange readable choreography without becoming copies of one another.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Most choreography communities rely heavily on:

  • memory
  • verbal teaching
  • video references
  • instructor interpretation

That works — until choreography is forgotten, altered, lost, or difficult to reproduce consistently.

The Saber Standard exists to make choreography portable.

A written sequence can be:

  • preserved
  • reconstructed
  • translated between instructors
  • reviewed years later
  • taught remotely
  • shared internationally
  • cited in manuals or curriculum

The goal is not to replace live teaching.

The goal is to make live teaching easier to preserve, repeat, and communicate.

docs.title: A shared language, not a franchise
docs.text:
The Saber Standard is intentionally designed to be broader than a single school.

SaberCraft is the founding school and original development community of the system, but the notation standard is meant to support a wider choreography ecosystem.

Schools using the Saber Standard should still feel like themselves.

Your:

  • ranking systems
  • costumes
  • lore
  • traditions
  • class structure
  • choreography style
  • performance philosophy

can remain entirely your own.

In this model, the notation language is shared while the choreography libraries remain independent.

docs.title: The long-term vision
docs.text:
The Saber Standard is being developed as:

  • a choreography notation standard
  • a preservation framework
  • a teaching reference language
  • a collaborative movement system
  • a public documentation standard for staged saber combat

The long-term goal is to help choreography communities preserve and exchange movement more clearly across schools, generations, and platforms.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: This glossary defines the working vocabulary of the Saber Standard. Terms are listed in roughly the order a new Saberist meets them, rather than alphabetically. Where a term has a page that introduces it in full, the term links there.

docs.title: The Saber Standard and its notation
docs.text:
These are the terms every Saberist uses, whether or not their school ever plays LUMINA Games.

Term Definition Saber Standard The choreography standard maintained by Lumina Federation LLC and originated through SaberCraft. Saberist The general practitioner term within the Saber Standard — anyone learning or performing Saber Standard choreography. Saberists Plural of Saberist. Target A numbered line or point used to describe the intended direction of an attack. Attack A choreographed movement toward an intended target point. Parry A defensive response to an attack. CM Choreography Movement; a reusable segment of a saber duel. CM Library The official baseline movement library. Telegraph A silent signal used to call or indicate a CM.

docs.title: LUMINA Games and advancement
docs.text:
These terms belong to the optional layers built on top of the Saber Standard. A Saberist can read, write, and teach choreography without using any of them.

Term Definition LUMINA Games Optional structured game/scoring format. Lumen A player within LUMINA Games specifically. Reserved for the Games layer — not used for general Saber Standard practitioners (see Saberist). Lumens Plural of Lumen (LUMINA Games players). Duel Two Saberists performing together. Knight A rank within the SaberCraft Knights program, an optional advancement system.

docs.title: The Saber Standard
docs.text:
The Saber Standard defines the public framework for documenting and teaching choreographed saber combat.

Standard vs. notation system

A notation system helps people write movement down: "here is how to write this move."

A standard does more. It gives the community a public rulebook — clear definitions, examples, updates, and a way to check whether choreography is being written correctly — so a community can agree on what that writing means.

The Saber Standard includes notation, but the goal is bigger: a public, maintained, reviewable standard for choreographed saber combat.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
The standard includes:

  • notation grammar
  • target and parry references
  • Choreography Movement structure
  • core movement library
  • telegraph conventions
  • optional game/rule structure
  • controlled glossary
  • licensing and attribution guidance

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
If a notation system is hard to find, locked behind old material, or depends on one instructor’s memory, groups eventually start making their own rules.

That is understandable.

But over time, it creates confusion.

One school may write a move one way. Another school may write the same move differently. Without a public reference, nobody knows which version is correct.

A standard helps prevent that.

docs.title: What makes a standard different?
docs.text: Feature Why it matters Public People can find it and read it Accessible Students and schools do not need private access to learn it Maintained Someone is responsible for keeping it updated Versioned Changes are tracked over time Reviewable Choreography can be checked for clarity and accuracy Reusable Schools can use it without joining one specific curriculum Durable The system is meant to last

docs.title: More than attack notation
docs.text:
Some notation systems mainly record attack targets. They can tell you where a strike is going, but they may not describe the rest of the scene.

That can create choreography that feels one-directional:

one person attacks, the other person reacts, then the next attack happens.

That can be useful for drills, but staged combat needs more.

A fight scene is not just saber direction. It is body movement, distance, rhythm, safety, reaction, and performance.

The Saber Standard is designed to capture the full choreographic exchange.

A Saber Standard sequence can include:

  • attacks
  • parries
  • defensive responses
  • ducks
  • turns
  • spins
  • jumps
  • recoils
  • locks
  • holds
  • thrusts
  • kicks
  • flourishes
  • transitions
  • timing between performers

Attack notation tells you where the saber goes. The Saber Standard is built to show what the whole choreography does.

docs.title: Why the Saber Standard is different
docs.text:
The Saber Standard is built from more than ten years of real practice.

The notation material has been available online for over a decade, and the current Saber Standard is being organized so it can remain publicly available as a long-term reference.

It was developed through SaberCraft, a school that has taught and refined saber choreography for more than a decade with a consistent student base.

That matters.

The Saber Standard did not come from theory alone. It came from real classes, real students, real choreography, and years of figuring out what people can actually learn, teach, remember, and perform safely.

docs.title: Built for more than one fandom
docs.text:
The Saber Standard may be inspired by saber culture, but it is not limited to one franchise.

It connects to:

  • theater
  • stage combat
  • martial arts-inspired movement
  • martial sports
  • partner choreography
  • performance safety
  • movement documentation
  • teaching systems

At its core, the Saber Standard is for people who care about process.

It is for instructors, performers, students, clubs, and schools that want choreography to be clear, repeatable, and teachable.

docs.title: Availability is part of the standard
docs.text:
A standard should not disappear.

It should not depend on unavailable videos, private notes, or one person’s memory.

The Saber Standard is designed to be available online, with documentation, examples, FAQs, updates, and public ways to ask questions.

That means students, teachers, and schools can use the same reference instead of guessing.

docs.title: Start Here
docs.text:
Welcome to the Saber Standard.

This page is the shortest safe path into the system. You do not need to understand the entire standard before you begin. You only need a partner, a safe training space, and enough notation to practice the first core movement: CM-A.

What the Saber Standard is

The Saber Standard is a lightsaber choreography standard. It is used to record, teach, share, and safely perform choreographed saber combat.

What the Saber Standard is not

The Saber Standard is not full-contact sparring, dueling, fencing, or combat training for real weapons. It is controlled partner choreography.

docs.title: 1. Start with CM-A
docs.text:
CM-A is the first core movement, and every step of it is written in Saber Standard Notation. Before you practice it, get familiar with how that notation reads.

Select the diagram above, or go straight to the Notation Overview.

Practising away from a screen? Print the Quick Start Guide — one page with the target diagrams and every core sequence on it.

docs.title: 2. Safety baseline
docs.text:
Before anything else, agree on safety.

A Saber Standard exchange should be practiced with control. The goal is not to hit your partner. The goal is to create a clean, readable, repeatable movement pattern together.

Minimum practice rules:

  • Use appropriate training sabers or safe props.
  • Check your distance with your partner before starting any sequence.
  • Make eye contact with your partner as the signal that you're both ready to begin.
  • Move slowly when learning.
  • Stop before contact.
  • Do not strike the body.
  • Do not surprise your partner.
  • Reset when either partner feels unsafe or confused.
  • Increase speed only after both partners understand the pattern.

If the movement is not safe, it is not correct.

docs.title: 3. Why use notation instead of video alone?
Video is powerful. But video alone is fragile.
docs.text:
Most choreography communities rely almost entirely on:

  • memory
  • demonstration
  • verbal explanation
  • recordings
  • instructor interpretation

That works well for short-term teaching.

But over time, choreography becomes difficult to preserve consistently.

Sequences change.

Details are forgotten.

Different instructors remember different versions.

Videos disappear.

Footwork becomes unclear.

Timing drifts.

And eventually, choreography that once existed clearly becomes fragmented or lost.

The Saber Standard was created to solve that problem.

docs.title: Choreography deserves a written language
docs.text:
A written notation system allows movement to become:

  • portable
  • archivable
  • teachable
  • searchable
  • repeatable
  • collaborative
  • easier to preserve over time

The goal is not to replace live teaching.

The goal is to support it.

Video shows performance.

Notation shows structure.

Together, they become far more powerful.

docs.title: Video and notation solve different problems
docs.text:
Video is good for… Notation is good for… Emotion and acting Structural clarity Timing feel Exact sequence reference Performance energy Step-by-step readability Watching movement Reconstructing movement Visual style Archival preservation Demonstration Cross-school communication

A video can inspire choreography.

Notation can preserve it.

docs.title: Why choreography gets lost
docs.text: Many choreography groups eventually encounter the same problems:

docs.title: "We used to teach that sequence differently."
docs.text: Without written notation, small changes accumulate over time.

docs.title: "I know the fight when I see it, but I can’t explain it clearly."
docs.text: A notation system creates a common teaching language.

docs.title: "The original instructor is gone."
docs.text: A written sequence survives beyond a single teacher.

docs.title: "The video angle doesn’t show enough detail."
docs.text: Notation can clarify attack lines, responses, timing, and structure.

docs.title: "Nobody remembers Version 1 anymore."
docs.text: Notation creates historical preservation.

docs.title: 4. The Saber Standard is designed for portability
docs.text:
The Saber Standard allows choreography to move between:

  • schools
  • instructors
  • teams
  • conventions
  • online communities
  • performance groups

A choreography written in Saber Standard Notation can be:

  • printed
  • translated into teaching material
  • reviewed during rehearsal
  • shared digitally
  • referenced years later

docs.title: 5. A shared language across schools
docs.text:
One of the goals of the Saber Standard is interoperability.

Different schools can keep their own:

  • curriculum
  • traditions
  • choreography libraries
  • aesthetics
  • teaching style

while still using a shared notation language.

This means choreography can become exchangeable without forcing communities to become identical.

docs.title: 6. A practical example
docs.text:
Imagine two schools:

  • SaberCraft
  • NY Kendo School

Each school has its own choreography library.

Without shared notation:

  • choreography transfer is difficult
  • verbal explanation becomes inconsistent
  • videos require interpretation
  • reconstruction takes longer

With the Saber Standard:

  • both schools can read the same notation grammar
  • choreography becomes easier to exchange
  • instructors can discuss movement more precisely
  • sequences become easier to archive and preserve

The choreography remains unique.

The language becomes shared.

docs.title: 7. Written choreography changes how communities grow
docs.text:
Once choreography can be documented consistently, communities gain the ability to:

  • build public archives
  • compare variations
  • preserve historical sequences
  • collaborate remotely
  • publish manuals
  • create structured curriculum
  • annotate revisions
  • standardize judging or review systems
  • maintain choreography across generations

This is one of the reasons notation systems transformed:

  • music
  • dance
  • engineering
  • mathematics
  • software development
  • martial systems

The Saber Standard applies that same philosophy to choreographed saber movement.

docs.title: 8. The long-term vision
docs.text:
The standard exists to help creativity survive.

The standard is designed to support a future where choreographed movement can be:

  • documented clearly
  • exchanged openly
  • preserved responsibly
  • taught consistently
  • studied historically
  • expanded collaboratively

Video captures motion.

Notation captures structure.

Together, they allow choreography to outlive memory alone.

docs.title: Why governance matters
docs.text:
The Saber Standard is intended to function as a long-term choreography notation standard.

To remain useful across schools, instructors, communities, and future releases, the standard needs:

  • stable terminology
  • documented revisions
  • controlled updates
  • version tracking
  • clear distinction between official and contributed material

This page defines the current governance model for the Saber Standard.

docs.title: Current standard version
docs.text:
Version Status Notes v1.0 Historical foundation Original assembled SaberCraft guide and system draft v2.0 Active Current public standard, hosted at standard.sabercraft.org

v2.0 is a finished, stable release. Saberists, instructors, and schools can teach and notate from it today; it is not a draft in progress.

docs.title: Governance philosophy
docs.text:
The Saber Standard is designed to evolve carefully.

The goal is to allow:

  • improvement
  • expansion
  • experimentation
  • community participation

without constantly breaking compatibility between schools and choreography archives.

Whenever possible:

  • notation should remain readable across versions
  • terminology changes should be documented
  • major structural changes should be deliberate

docs.title: Stewardship
docs.text:
The Saber Standard is currently:

  • developed by the SaberCraft community
  • maintained by Lumina Federation LLC
  • published publicly at standard.sabercraft.org

SaberCraft serves as the founding school and original implementation community of the standard.

docs.title: Official versus community material
docs.text:
Not all choreography or notation material carries the same authority level.

Category Meaning Official Approved baseline Saber Standard material Extended Official expansions beyond the beginner baseline Community Independent or contributed material written using the Saber Standard

This structure allows schools and instructors to innovate without immediately changing the official baseline.

docs.title: Change philosophy
docs.text:
Small improvements are expected over time.

Examples include:

  • clarifying terminology
  • improving diagrams
  • refining beginner explanations
  • documenting notation edge cases
  • expanding examples

Large structural changes should be approached carefully.

Examples include:

  • changing target numbering
  • redefining notation grammar
  • breaking compatibility with older choreography
  • changing table structure conventions

docs.title: Public reference model
docs.text:
The official public reference for the standard currently includes:

  • GitHub repository
  • Markdown source files
  • version-controlled history
  • public documentation site
  • downloadable releases in the future

This structure is intended to improve transparency, preservation, and long-term maintainability.

docs.title: Advancement
docs.text:
Completely optional

Advancement is an add-on, not a requirement. Any organization using the Saber Standard is free to adopt it as a way to add another dimension to what it offers, and equally free to leave it aside. It has nothing to do with adopting the notation: reading, writing, and teaching Saber Standard Notation calls for no rank, sash, or program of any kind.

Advancement covers the ranking and recognition programs built on top of the Saber Standard.

The program documented here is the SaberCraft Knights program, run by SaberCraft, the founding school. Knights gain rank and are recognized in any LUMINA or SaberCraft-based school or club.

docs.title: SaberCraft Knights
docs.text:
Saberists may reach a point where they want to test their skills and take on the road to Saber Mastery.

Saber Mastery is harder than many expect. Performing saber choreography from memory, and improvising combinations on the fly, takes dedicated training and commitment. The aim is to make saber play second nature while staying mindful of your movement and your safety.

Being a Knight is about contributing to the future of SaberCraft and its students. The Knights Program empowers people who want to learn saber choreography while adopting principles of wellness into their lives. Through it, members develop Saber Mastery and leadership while building a positive wellness and fitness routine.

docs.title: Knight sashes
docs.text:
Based on established martial arts programs, the Knights program uses a curriculum with a rank system built on merit and personal accomplishment. Ranks are designated with sashes, using the same sashes available for other martial arts.

Sash Rank Requirements White Honorary Knight For contributors who have helped SaberCraft in a meaningful way, without needing to demonstrate knowledge of the CMs Yellow Initiate Knight (1) Involved with SaberCraft for a minimum of 6 months or sessions, or proficiency with 5 CMs. The first sash granted to students advancing through the ranks Orange Scribe Knight (2) A minimum of 12 months or sessions, or proficiency with 10 or more CMs. Also contributes to class, including coordinating and helping with setup and takedown, and has taken part in at least one external event Indigo Keeper Knight (3) A minimum of 24 months or sessions, proficiency with 15 or more CMs, and conducting group instruction or event participation. Has also participated in LUMINA Green Master Knight (4) A minimum of 36 months or sessions, proficiency with 20 or more CMs, and conducting group instruction or event participation. Has also completed and judged several LUMINA games or seasons Red Instructor Knight (5) A minimum of 36 months or sessions, proficiency with 15 or more CMs, competed in one season of LUMINA, taught a minimum of 5 group sessions, and completed a fitness certification. Regular participants, judges, and coordinators of LUMINA

docs.title: Testing your skills
docs.text:
Those enrolled in the program have access to exams that test their skills and open up leadership roles in classes and community events, including workshops.

Rather than practising with others occasionally, or whenever partners can make the time, the Knights program means there are like-minded people setting aside time to practise their saber craft fully. You dedicate yourself to the art and to your practice. It can mean arriving a little earlier to help out, or taking on a new student and working through a particular form with them. For some it is about community events; for others it is a sense of accomplishment.

Each level of Knight has a number of CMs they must commit to. These may be demonstrated by successful attack and defence, either in a class demonstration or in a recorded LUMINA battle.

Knights who are grandfathered in may opt to take the legacy tests. Knights who are grandfathered in manually, and new Knights, cannot take the old tests.

docs.title: Time requirements
docs.text:
Time is defined by a minimum number of sessions. As classes are monthly, a requirement of 6 months means either 6 months of attendance, or however many months it takes to reach 6 sessions.

Sessions are cumulative and linked to rank. A Yellow Knight who has attended 6 months needs only a further 6 months of attendance to qualify for Orange.

docs.title: Age requirements and disqualifications
docs.text:
Age requirements, and the conditions that lead to disqualification, are set by each school or club running the program rather than by the Saber Standard. Saber combat is a delicate dance, so safety is the highest priority.

SaberCraft's own conditions are documented at disqualifications from the Knight program and general disqualifications.

docs.title: Becoming a Knight
docs.text:
Knights start by showing up to class regularly and asking to join. To join, a candidate completes the following:

  1. Preliminary steps. Complete 6 months of classes, or 6 sessions.
  2. Ask to join. Talk to one of the Knights and mention that you are interested. After a brief interview with several Knights, they discuss it among themselves and your membership goes to a vote with those who interviewed you. A simple majority welcomes you in.
  3. Test and pass rank 1. The final step before you join, demonstrating that you understand the minimum number of CMs needed for recognition in a rank.

Sashes are optional. Holding Knight recognition is free, and a suggested donation of $24 per rank covers the cost of a sash. Schools and Saberists are equally free to source their own sashes and award them. Enrolling in the Knights program is not required to be part of SaberCraft; it is for those who want tokens of advancement.

docs.title: Acceptance and voting
docs.text:
Candidates who wish to become Knights are voted in. For each candidate, a team of Electors is chosen at random to vote on whether the candidate may become a Knight. Randomising the Electors prevents control by a total majority, or by cliques that may develop.

Most candidates are expected to be accepted. Where a candidate is rejected, there should be a clear reason.

  1. Each round of candidates is reviewed by the instructors, who are encouraged to seek a consensus among active Knights on whether there is a reason the candidate should not join. Any voice of dissent must come with a reason.
  2. The instructors review the case and may either reject the candidate early, or abstain and forward the information to the Elector Knights. Instructors may interview others involved in the rejection, and may interview the candidate to hear a rebuttal.
  3. A group of randomly assigned Knights forms the Electors, who vote on the candidate.
  4. If approved, the instructors purchase the sash and schedule a presentation date, verifying the candidate will be present.
  5. If rejected, an instructor informs the candidate why they were not accepted for the program.

docs.title: Choreography Movements (CM)
docs.text:
Choreography Movements are reusable sequences of saber duels. Each movement is a short, repeatable sequence that can be taught, practiced, written in notation, combined with other movements, and performed the same way by Saberists anywhere.

Each movement is identified by a CM code, such as CM-A or CM-B. "CM" is short for Choreography Movement — the original name for these building blocks.

docs.title: Where to Start
docs.text:
If you are new to the Saber Standard, focus on the first five movements: CM-A through CM-E. These establish the shared vocabulary, timing, targeting, attack lines, parries, and partner discipline that everything else builds on.

All five are documented right here. CM-A shows how notation becomes a real, teachable paired movement; CM-B extends it into the four angle target points; CM-C introduces completes across two parts — the completes themselves first, then the full choreography; CM-D starts trading the attack between Saberists; and CM-E adds special moves and a second opponent.

The full movement library is organized below into three tiers, each with its own page: Core Library, Extended Library, and Community Library.

docs.title: How the Movement Library Is Organized
docs.text:
The movement library is organized into three levels, so you always know how official a movement is:

Library What it holds Status Core The baseline movements every Saberist learns first. As a new student, this is your home — start with CM-A through CM-E. Official Extended Official movements that go beyond the beginner foundation, introducing more complex timing, footwork, transitions, reversals, counters, and cinematic phrasing. Explore these once you are comfortable with the Core movements. Official Community Movements developed and contributed by Saberists, schools, clubs, and partner communities. Community movements are clearly marked and credit their contributors. Over time, some may be promoted into the Extended or Core libraries. Community-reviewed

docs.title: CM-A
docs.text:
CM-A is the first official core movement in the Saber Standard.

It teaches the most basic relationship in Saber Standard Notation:

attack line → matching parry

CM-A should be the first paired sequence taught to new Saberists.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
Player Step 1 Step 2 Step 3 Step 4 Step 5 Step 6 Saberist A 1 11 3 9 5 7 Saberist B 1P 11P 3P 9P 5P 7P

Read each column vertically. Saberist A performs the attack listed in the top row. Saberist B performs the matching parry listed in the bottom row.

A plain number is an attack toward that target line. The same number followed by P is the parry that receives it — so every column of CM-A is the same line answered on both sides.

docs.title: Telegraph
docs.text:
Fist pointed out at your opponent (ASL-A).

The telegraph is the silent signal that calls CM-A before an exchange begins. See LUMINA Games for how telegraphs are used in play.

docs.title: The six target points
docs.text:
CM-A runs on the six beginner target lines:

Target Beginner description 1 High / upper center line 11 High opposite line 3 Side line 9 Opposite side line 5 Low line 7 Opposite low line

Targets are named from the attacker's perspective: the clock face sits on the partner, and the number is read from the attacking side. A target number does not mean "hit this body part" — it means "move toward this choreographed line."

These six are enough to read and practice CM-A. Fuller explanations live in Targets, Attacks, and Parries; the complete twelve-line reference is in the Notation Legend.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-A is designed to teach:

  • the six beginner target lines
  • the meaning of P as parry
  • the two-row notation format
  • safe attack/parry timing
  • role awareness between Saberist A and Saberist B
  • clean repetition before speed

CM-A is not a performance sequence by itself. It is a foundation drill.

docs.title: Phase 1: Static walkthrough
docs.text:
Move one step at a time.

After each step, pause and confirm:

  • both Saberists know the target line
  • the parry matches the attack
  • distance is safe
  • the movement can be repeated

Do not rush this phase. This is where the pattern becomes clear.

docs.title: Phase 2: Slow continuous flow
docs.text:
Perform all six steps without stopping.

Keep the movement slow enough that both Saberists can read every line.

If either Saberist loses the sequence, stop and restart from Step 1.

docs.title: Phase 3: Role switch
docs.text:
Switch roles.

Now Saberist B performs the attack row and Saberist A performs the parry row.

Both Saberists should learn both sides of CM-A.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-A should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

The teacher's job is to help both Saberists understand the notation, recognize the target lines, and build safe timing together.

A fast CM-A is not automatically a good CM-A. A good CM-A is clear, controlled, and repeatable — all six steps in order, each parry matching its written attack, performed without verbal correction.

When CM-A is clean, continue to CM-B, which takes the same attack-and-parry relationship into the four angle target points.

docs.title: CM-B
docs.text:
CM-B is the second core movement in the Saber Standard: angle attacks on targets 2, 10, 4, and 8.

Where CM-A works the upright lines, CM-B moves the exchange into the corners — the shoulder and hip angles.

The diagram shows those four points highlighted. Select it to open it full size in a new tab.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
Player Step 1 Step 2 Step 3 Step 4 Step 5 Step 6 Step 7 Step 8 Saberist A 2 10 4 8 2 10 4 8 Saberist B 2P 10P 4P 8P 2P 10P 4P 8P

The four angle points run twice. Steps 5 through 8 repeat steps 1 through 4 exactly.

docs.title: Telegraph
docs.text:
Palm pointed out at your opponent, all fingers pointing up (ASL-B).

The telegraph is the silent signal that calls CM-B before an exchange begins. See LUMINA Games for how telegraphs are used in play.

docs.title: The four angle points
docs.text:
CM-A introduces six target lines. CM-B adds four more:

Target Corner Angle 2 Upper corner Shoulder-height angle 10 Opposite upper corner Shoulder-height angle 4 Lower corner Hip-height angle 8 Opposite lower corner Hip-height angle

These four points are the whole of CM-B — every step in the movement lands on one of them.

They are also what completes the Saber Standard target model. With the corners in play, a Saberist can write and read a diagonal exchange in the same notation used for a vertical or horizontal one, and choreography no longer has to be described in words when it leaves the upright lines. That is the practical reason the angle points matter: they make the notation cover the full clock face rather than a subset of it.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-B is designed to teach:

  • the four angle target lines
  • diagonal attack and parry pairing
  • the corner-to-corner rhythm of upper and lower angles
  • a repeating eight-step sequence
  • angle recovery between shoulder and hip height
  • role awareness between Saberist A and Saberist B

Like CM-A, CM-B is a foundation drill rather than a performance sequence.

docs.title: Phase 1: Static walkthrough
docs.text:
Move one step at a time.

After each step, pause and confirm:

  • both Saberists know which corner is being attacked
  • the parry matches the angle, not just the height
  • distance is safe
  • the movement can be repeated

The two upper angles and the two lower angles are easy to confuse early on. Name the target out loud until the corners are obvious to both Saberists.

docs.title: Phase 2: Slow continuous flow
docs.text:
Perform all eight steps without stopping.

Keep the movement slow enough that both Saberists can read every line. The transition from step 4 back into step 5 — lower corner returning to upper corner — is where the sequence most often breaks. Practice that seam on its own if needed.

If either Saberist loses the sequence, stop and restart from Step 1.

docs.title: Phase 3: Role switch
docs.text:
Switch roles.

Now Saberist B performs the attack row and Saberist A performs the parry row.

Both Saberists should learn both sides of CM-B.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-B should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

Angle attacks travel further than upright ones, so distance discipline matters more here than in CM-A. Reset the pair rather than letting a wide angle close the gap.

Once CM-B is clean, both Saberists have ten of the twelve target lines available, and longer combinations can be written that move freely between upright and angled attacks.

When CM-B is clean, continue to CM-C Part 1, which introduces swings that carry through instead of stopping.

docs.title: CM-C — Part 1: Completes
docs.text:
Part 1 of CM-C teaches a single idea: some swings stop at the target, and some swings carry through.

Learn this before attempting the full movement in Part 2. The choreography there cannot be read — or performed safely — without it.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
A complete is written by adding the © symbol to the target line.

Symbol Meaning 1© Complete on the 1 line 5© Complete on the 5 line 12© Complete on the 12 line

These three are the completes covered in this lesson. The full symbol list is in the Notation Legend.

docs.title: Completes and Complete Across
docs.text:
A Complete is a wide arc swing that flows through uninterrupted.

A Complete Across is a wide arc swing committed at a particular target point, but travelling parallel to the ground.

Both are written with the © symbol, which marks the swing as uninterrupted.

That distinction is what Part 1 exists to teach, and it is one of the things that sets Saber Standard Notation apart. Most ways of writing choreography record where a swing is aimed. Saber Standard Notation records where it is aimed and whether it stops there. 5 and 5© name the same line and describe two different actions: one arrives at the target and holds; the other keeps going.

The consequence shows up in the defence. A stopping attack can be met with a parry on the same line. A complete cannot — there is nothing to hold against, so the defender has to move instead. A fight written without the © symbol is a fight that records parries the choreography cannot actually perform.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Part 1 is designed to teach:

  • the difference between a stopping attack and a complete
  • what a Complete Across adds to that idea
  • the © symbol and when a swing earns it
  • reading 5 and 5© as two different instructions
  • why a complete changes what the defender can do
  • the space and control a carrying arc demands

docs.title: Phase 1: Feel the difference
docs.text:
Working alone, with no partner in front of you, take one line — the 5 line is a good start.

Perform it twice: once stopping at the target, once carrying through as 5©.

Repeat until the two feel like different actions rather than the same action at different speeds.

docs.title: Phase 2: Read and perform
docs.text:
Have a partner call symbols at random from 1, 1©, 5, 5©, 12, and 12©.

Perform what is called, still without a partner standing in the line of the swing.

The goal is recognition: seeing or hearing © should change what you do without having to think about it.

docs.title: Phase 3: Add the defender
docs.text:
Only now bring a partner in, at a distance that leaves the arc clear.

Saberist A performs a called complete. Saberist B does not parry it — B moves out of its path.

Reset the distance between every repetition.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
Teach the symbol before teaching the swing.

Once a Saberist can read the difference between 5 and 5© on the page, the movement follows naturally. A Saberist who has only been shown the swing will keep reaching for a parry that is not available.

The safety rule for this lesson is simple and does not bend: a complete does not stop, so nothing but distance and the defender's movement clears the blade. Keep the arc empty until both Saberists are certain of the line.

When completes are clear, continue to Part 2.

docs.title: CM-C — Part 2: Choreography
docs.text:
Part 2 is the full CM-C movement. It opens with the six upright lines of CM-A, then breaks out of them into the completes taught in Part 1.

Do not start here. The second half of this movement is unreadable without ©.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 s9 s10 Saberist A 1 11 3 9 5 7 2© 9 5© 12© Saberist B 1P 11P 3P 9P 5P 7P Crouch 9PM6 Jump

Steps 1 through 6 are the CM-A attack/parry pairs. From step 7 the movement changes character:

  • 2©, 5©, and 12© are completes — the swing carries through rather than stopping.
  • A complete is not met with a parry. Saberist B answers 2© with a crouch and 5© with a jump, letting the arc pass.
  • 9PM6 is a parry with a modifier — see below.
  • Saberist B has no listed response to the closing 12©. The sequence ends on Saberist A's complete.

docs.title: Telegraph
docs.text:
Forward Flourish.

The telegraph is the silent signal that calls CM-C before an exchange begins. See LUMINA Games for how telegraphs are used in play.

docs.title: The M modifier
docs.text:
Part 2 adds a parameter to a defence.

When a number follows P, the M designator specifies where the tip of the saber points for that defensive pose. 9PM6 is a 9 parry, modified so the blade points down at the 6 position.

The posture guards one side of the body while appearing to answer a strike from behind — the same shape reads two ways, which is exactly the kind of thing choreography needs to be able to write down.

The modifier is what lets one parry line cover several distinct poses without inventing new symbols for each. The full symbol list, including © and M, is in the Notation Legend.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Part 2 is designed to teach:

  • a full ten-step movement combining stopping attacks and completes
  • evasion as a legitimate answer to an attack
  • the M modifier and blade-tip position in a parry
  • switching response type mid-sequence
  • moving from the familiar CM-A opening into unfamiliar territory
  • role awareness between Saberist A and Saberist B

docs.title: Phase 1: Static walkthrough
docs.text:
Run steps 1 through 6 first. These are CM-A and should already be clean.

Then take steps 7 through 10 one at a time. After each, pause and confirm:

  • Saberist A knows whether the swing stops or completes
  • Saberist B knows whether the answer is a parry, a crouch, or a jump
  • the arc has room to travel without reaching Saberist B
  • the movement can be repeated

Completes need more space than stopping attacks. Set the distance before adding any speed.

docs.title: Phase 2: Slow continuous flow
docs.text:
Perform all ten steps without stopping.

The seam at step 7 is where the sequence usually breaks: Saberist B has just parried six attacks in a row and must now stop parrying and drop instead. Practice steps 6 and 7 together until the change of response is automatic.

If either Saberist loses the sequence, stop and restart from Step 1.

docs.title: Phase 3: Role switch
docs.text:
Switch roles.

Now Saberist B performs the attack row and Saberist A performs the parry row.

Both Saberists should learn both sides of CM-C.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-C should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

The safety change from CM-A and CM-B is real: a complete does not stop, so the defender's evasion is the only thing that clears the blade. Neither Saberist should attempt steps 7 through 10 at speed until both can perform them slowly, in the right order, without discussion.

If a pair struggles with the second half, the problem is usually Part 1 rather than this sequence. Send them back to completes and return when 5 and 5© read as different instructions.

When CM-C is clean, continue to CM-D, where the attack starts changing hands.

docs.title: CM Catalog
docs.text:
The CM Catalog is the flat index of every Choreography Movement in the Saber Standard — what each one is, which fight it interprets, and who notated it.

The Core, Extended, and Community libraries are the teaching path: they tell you what to learn and in what order. This page is the lookup table. Use it when you know roughly what you are after — a CM letter, a film, a character, a contributor — and want to find it quickly.

Entire battles can be notated by any school and shared. From those fights, specific movements are selected and added to the Saber Standard libraries. See Community Library for how to contribute one.

docs.text:
The film, series, character, and performer names in these tables are descriptive references only. They identify which filmed sequence a given choreography interprets. Nothing here claims ownership of, affiliation with, sponsorship by, or endorsement by the rights holders of those works, and all such names and marks remain the property of their respective owners.

docs.title: CM-D
docs.text:
CM-D is the fourth core movement in the Saber Standard, and the first one that is a conversation rather than a lecture.

In CM-A through CM-C, one Saberist attacks and the other defends for the whole sequence. In CM-D the attack changes hands repeatedly, so both Saberists trade strikes instead of one delivering all of them.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
CM-D is written in two tables. The first is the exchange; the second is the finish.

The exchange

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 s9 s10 Saberist A 1 11 2P 10P 3 9 4P 8P 5 7 Saberist B 1P 11P 2 10 3P 9P 4 8 5P 7P

Read down each column as usual, but watch which row carries the P. At steps 1–2 Saberist A attacks. At steps 3–4 the P moves to A's row and Saberist B attacks. The roles change again at steps 5–6, 7–8, and 9–10.

The lines themselves are borrowed from movements already learned: the upright lines of CM-A and the angle points of CM-B.

The finish

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 Saberist A 12 Turn 180 3PM6 Step-through turn 180 Pose Saberist B Left/Blend Turn 180 0 Step-through turn 180 Pose

The finish adds a turn, a thrust, and a shared closing pose. 3PM6 is a 3 parry modified so the blade points down at 6 — the same modifier introduced in CM-C Part 2.

docs.title: Telegraph
docs.text:
Reverse Flourish.

The telegraph is the silent signal that calls CM-D before an exchange begins. See LUMINA Games for how telegraphs are used in play.

docs.title: Dynamic combat
docs.text:
CM-D builds a dialog between two opponents. By switching who is the attacker, two Saberists trade strikes rather than one performing every attack — and because the sequence draws its lines from CM-A, CM-B, and CM-C, the switching is the only genuinely new demand.

That is what makes CM-D the bridge movement. A fight is not a list of attacks answered in turn; it is an exchange where initiative passes back and forth. CM-D is the first movement that writes that down.

CM-D also introduces two notation elements.

docs.title: Thrusts
docs.text:
A thrust is noted by a 0 (zero) in the notation. Saberist B delivers one at step 3 of the finish.

A thrust travels along a different path from a cut, so it needs its own symbol rather than a target number alone.

docs.title: Unconventional blocks
docs.text:
CM-D introduces blocks taken at an alternative angle to the one the attack would normally invite.

3PM6 is the example: the parry holds the 3 line, but the blade points down at 6 rather than up. The defence is sound, and it reads differently to an audience — which is the point of writing the angle down rather than leaving it to the performer.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-D is designed to teach:

  • switching between attacker and defender mid-sequence
  • reading which row carries the P to find the current attacker
  • thrusts, noted 0
  • unconventional block angles
  • combining lines drawn from CM-A, CM-B, and CM-C
  • turning, stepping through, and finishing together in a pose

docs.title: Phase 1: Static walkthrough
docs.text:
Run the exchange table two steps at a time — one attacker's pair before the switch.

At every switch, pause and confirm:

  • both Saberists know who is attacking next
  • the incoming parry matches the written line
  • distance is safe through the change of role
  • the movement can be repeated

The handover is the whole lesson. Do not move on until each switch is deliberate rather than a scramble.

docs.title: Phase 2: Slow continuous flow
docs.text:
Perform all ten steps of the exchange without stopping, then add the finish.

Keep the movement slow enough that both Saberists can read every line. If a switch collapses, restart from Step 1 rather than resuming mid-exchange — the rhythm of the handover is what is being practiced.

docs.title: Phase 3: Role switch
docs.text:
Switch roles.

Because CM-D already trades the attack, this phase is subtler than in earlier movements: each Saberist now performs the other's half of every handover.

Both Saberists should learn both sides of CM-D.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-D should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

The most common error is treating the sequence as ten attacks with ten parries. It is five short exchanges, each with an owner. Teach it in pairs of steps, and the shape becomes obvious.

Watch distance through the turns in the finish. Both Saberists turn away and back, and a pair that was safely spaced before the turn can be too close after it.

When CM-D is clean, continue to CM-E, which adds special moves and a second opponent.

docs.title: CM-E
docs.text:
CM-E is the fifth and last core movement in the Saber Standard.

It is a quick movement that combines multiple partner attacks, and it works as either a 1-on-1 or a 2-on-1 scenario. Special moves act as milestones between switching partners.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
CM-E is written in two tables — one for each half of the exchange.

First exchange

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 Saberist A 9 4 8 5 11 3X Special Saberist B 9P 4P 8P 5P 11P 3X

Second exchange

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 Saberist A 2P 10P 3P 7P 1X Special Saberist B or C 2 10 3 7 1X

Three things to read carefully:

  • The roles invert between tables. Saberist A attacks through the first exchange and defends through the second.
  • X is a lock. It appears in both rows at the same step, because a lock is something the two Saberists do together rather than one doing to the other.
  • The third row label is a choice. Saberist B or C is what makes CM-E a 2-on-1 movement: the second exchange may be answered by the same partner or by a new one stepping in.

docs.title: Telegraph
docs.text:
Saber goes horizontally across the chest in a slow cut.

The telegraph is the silent signal that calls CM-E before an exchange begins. See LUMINA Games for how telegraphs are used in play.

docs.title: Special moves and counters
docs.text:
CM-E introduces the special move: a step written into the notation as Special rather than as a target line.

Each exchange runs a short series of attacks, closes into a lock, and resolves with a special move. The special move is a milestone — it marks the seam where partners switch, and it is where a movement stops being a drill and starts being a performance.

Because the notation names the slot without prescribing its contents, CM-E is the first movement that leaves a decision to the Saberists performing it. What fills a Special is chosen for the scene being built; what the notation guarantees is that both Saberists know a special move belongs there, and when.

The lock at 3X and 1X is what sets it up. A lock brings the exchange to a standstill and gives both Saberists a shared, stationary moment — the natural place to change partners or resolve.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-E is designed to teach:

  • combining attacks from multiple partners in one movement
  • 1-on-1 and 2-on-1 scenarios from the same notation
  • locks, noted X
  • the Special slot and where it belongs in a sequence
  • switching partners at a written milestone
  • inverting attacker and defender between exchanges

docs.title: Phase 1: Static walkthrough
docs.text:
Run each exchange separately, and run it 1-on-1 before attempting 2-on-1.

Take the attacks one at a time, then set the lock deliberately. After each step, confirm:

  • both Saberists know who is attacking in this exchange
  • the lock is entered with control, not collided into
  • distance is safe
  • the movement can be repeated

Decide what the special move will be before running the sequence. Do not improvise it during practice.

docs.title: Phase 2: Slow continuous flow
docs.text:
Perform both exchanges without stopping, still 1-on-1.

The seam is the lock into the special move. Practice steps 5 through 7 of the first exchange on their own until the transition out of the lock is smooth.

If either Saberist loses the sequence, stop and restart from Step 1.

docs.title: Phase 3: Add the second opponent
docs.text:
Only once the 1-on-1 version is clean, bring in Saberist C for the second exchange.

The incoming Saberist must know the whole sequence, not just their own entry. Walk the switch statically before running it.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-E should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

Two hazards belong to this movement specifically. A lock puts two Saberists at close quarters with blades engaged, so it is entered slowly and by agreement. And a 2-on-1 exchange means someone is moving into the space while an exchange is already live — that entry is choreographed, never spontaneous.

CM-E completes the Core Library. When it is clean, both Saberists have the shared vocabulary that every later movement builds on, and the Extended Library is open.

docs.title: CM-F
docs.text:
CM-F is the contactless movement, and the first step into the Extended Library.

One Saberist answers every attack with footwork and body movement instead of a blade. The other carries the saber and delivers the attacks, so the movement drills evasion on one side and controlled, safe swings on the other. The object is a continuous series of dodges.

For performance it reads two ways. It can show a character who controls the fight by demonstrating that they do not need a saber to engage — or a weaponless character avoiding strikes in order to escape, reach a weapon, or reach whatever else the scene requires.

CM-F was contributed by Santiago Martinez.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
CM-F is written in two tables: the opening, and the run that follows it.

Wide tables

Both tables below are wide. On a phone, turn the device landscape; either table can also be scrolled sideways.

The opening

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 Saberist A Blend-4 Crouched F-Duck Turn 180 Right Blend 3 Left Blend 3 Left Blend-4 Crouched F-Duck Saberist B Charge 2© Pass/turn 180 Right 12, turn 90 Left 12, turn 90 Left Turn Left with 2©

The run — performed throughout while stepping backwards.

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 s9 Saberist A Blend 1 Left Turn to Face Blend 1 Right Duck Blend 1 Left Jump Back Blend 3 Right Blend 1 Left Disarm Saberist B 12 Turn to Face 12 Spin L>R 10© 0 9© 12 0

Read down each column as usual, but notice what is missing: there is not a single P anywhere in the notation.

  • Only Saberist B's row carries target numbers. Every cell in Saberist A's row is a movement — a blend, a duck, a jump, a turn.
  • © is a complete, the same symbol taught in CM-C. The swing carries through rather than stopping, which is what gives Saberist A an arc to move around.
  • 0 is a thrust, as in CM-D.
  • Bl- is a blend in the Notation Legend; this movement writes it out in full, with the line it works on and the direction it travels — Blend 1 Left.
  • Step 2 of each table is shared. Both Saberists turn at the same moment — Turn 180 Right against Pass/turn 180 Right in the opening, and Turn to Face in both rows of the run.

docs.title: Telegraph
docs.text:
Saberist A version: two arms held out to the side, parallel. Saberist B version: put the saber away and taunt.

Either version calls CM-F. Agree which one you are using before the exchange begins.

The telegraph is the silent signal that calls CM-F before an exchange begins. See LUMINA Games for how telegraphs are used in play.

docs.title: Blending and disarms
docs.text:
Everything in the Core Library answers an attack by meeting it. A 1 is answered by a 1P; the blades make contact and stop each other. CM-F removes that option and asks what is left.

What is left is the blend. A blend takes the line of the incoming attack and moves the body off it rather than putting steel in its way, so the attack passes through the space the defender has already left. It is written Bl- in the Notation Legend, and here it carries both the line and the direction: Blend 1 Left blends the 1 line, travelling left.

Two things follow from that, and they are the reason this movement exists.

The first is that the defending Saberist has to read the attack earlier. A parry can be late and still work. A blend cannot — the body has to be moving before the blade arrives, which means the defender is reading the swing rather than reacting to it.

The second is that the attacking Saberist becomes responsible for the movement. There is no blade to stop a swing that goes wrong, so every attack in Saberist B's row is delivered at a distance and a speed that Saberist A can leave in time. This is why CM-F is as much a control drill for the armed Saberist as an evasion drill for the unarmed one.

The run also travels. The entire second table is performed stepping backwards, so the pair covers ground continuously while the sequence plays out — the defender giving way, the attacker following.

The last column is where it resolves. Saberist B thrusts (0) and Saberist A answers with a Disarm. Everything before it is avoidance; the disarm is the point at which avoidance turns into an answer, and it is what makes CM-F a scene rather than a run of dodges.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-F is designed to teach:

  • answering an attack without blade contact
  • blends, noted Bl-, and the line and direction each one carries
  • footwork and body movement as a complete defence
  • reading an attack early enough to leave its line
  • swing control and safe distance for the attacking Saberist
  • continuous movement backwards through a sequence
  • closing a movement with a disarm

docs.title: The disarm
docs.text:
The disarm is CM-F's special move — the milestone the movement builds to, in the sense CM-E introduces. It is the one moment in CM-F where the unarmed Saberist stops avoiding and acts, and it is what the whole run of blends is arranged to earn.

Practice it on its own, statically, before it goes anywhere near the run. Set the thrust and the disarm as a pair, slowly and by agreement, and repeat it until the hand-off is the same every time. Only add it to the sequence once it is.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-F should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

Two hazards belong to this movement specifically. The unarmed Saberist has nothing to stop a swing with, so the safety of the whole movement sits with the Saberist holding the saber — every attack is a controlled arc at a measured distance, and speed is added only when both sides are clean. And the run travels backwards across the floor, so the space behind Saberist A is checked before every repetition, not once at the start.

CM-F is also the first movement where a Saberist performs a full sequence with no weapon in hand. That is worth naming to students: the notation is a language for choreographed movement, not for swordplay alone, and a row without a single target number in it is still notation.

When CM-F is clean, continue to CM-G, which takes the exchange into saber locking, or return to the Extended Library.

docs.title: CM-G
docs.text:
CM-G is the locking movement, and the second lesson in the Extended Library.

It interprets the duel between father and son in Star Wars: Return of the Jedi. No official notation exists for that fight, so what is written here is one reading of it, and in places the order of the filmed moments has been rearranged so the sequence tells a clean choreographed story rather than following the cut of the film.

What makes CM-G its own lesson is the locks. They arrive in the first few steps and recur throughout, and every one of them is a point where the exchange stops moving. Those stops are the movement's real subject: they are what let a pair hold a beat, play a moment of struggle, and give a long fight its pacing.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
CM-G runs eleven steps in a single table.

Wide tables

The table below is wide. On a phone, turn the device landscape; the table can also be scrolled sideways.

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 s9 s10 s11 Saberist A 0 X X, Pull R 10© 2© 5X 1 11 11X 9© 9© Saberist B 3P>9PX 9P, S+S: Pull L X Duck Duck 5X 1P 11P 11PX Dodge Dodge

Read down each column as usual, and notice how often both rows hold the same thing at the same time.

  • X is a lock, the symbol introduced in CM-E. It appears in both rows at the same step, because a lock is something two Saberists do together rather than one doing to the other.
  • S+S is a saber stand-off — a lock held rather than broken. Steps 1 to 3 are one continuous engagement: the thrust is parried into a lock, the lock is held, and each Saberist pulls away from it in a different direction.
  • 3P>9PX reads left to right. Saberist B parries the thrust on the 3 line, carries that parry up to 9, and finishes the movement in a lock.
  • 0 is a thrust, as in CM-D.
  • © is a complete, taught in CM-C. The swing carries through the target instead of stopping at it.
  • Not every attack is answered with a blade. Duck and Dodge fill Saberist B's row at steps 4, 5, 10 and 11 — a completed swing is travelling too far to be met, so it is left instead.
  • There are three locks in the movement: the stand-off at steps 2 and 3, 5X at step 6, and 11X at step 9. They divide the eleven steps into short bursts of exchange separated by stillness.

docs.title: Telegraph
docs.text:
A forward eight flourish, or a helicopter flourish into Position 3.

Either version calls CM-G. Agree which one you are using before the exchange begins.

The telegraph is the silent signal that calls CM-G before an exchange begins. See LUMINA Games for how telegraphs are used in play.

docs.title: Locks and stand-offs
docs.text:
A lock is written X, and it is the one thing in the notation that neither Saberist performs alone. Two blades meet and stay met. Nothing advances until the lock is released, so a lock is a shared decision as much as a shared position.

CM-E puts a single lock at the end of each exchange, where it marks a seam. CM-G does something different: it builds a whole movement out of them. Three locks break eleven steps into four short runs of blade work, and the movement spends as much time held as it does moving.

That is the lesson. A long exchange performed at one continuous speed has no shape to it — everything reads as equally important, and an audience has nowhere to rest. Locks give a fight its punctuation. Each one stops the sequence at a chosen moment, holds the two Saberists face to face, and then lets the exchange restart from a new footing.

The stand-off at the opening is where this is clearest. Saberist A thrusts, Saberist B parries the thrust on the 3 line and carries the parry up to 9, and the two finish bound together. S+S marks that bind as prolonged — not a lock that is broken as soon as it forms, but one that is deliberately held. Both Saberists then pull, in opposite directions: Saberist B to the left, Saberist A to the right. The pull is what makes a stand-off read as a struggle rather than a pause. Neither Saberist is waiting; both are working, and the tension is visible.

The two later locks work faster. 5X at step 6 catches a low attack and stops the exchange dead in the middle of the movement. 11X at step 9 catches a high one and sets up the finish. Both are entered from an attack that is met rather than parried away, which is why the notation carries the target number into the lock: 5X is a lock on the 5 line, 11PX is a parry on the 11 line that becomes one.

Entering a lock safely is the whole technique. The blades come together at a controlled speed, at a controlled angle, at a distance both Saberists have agreed on before the sequence starts. A lock is never collided into. Leaving one is the same in reverse: the release is choreographed, both Saberists know which way each is going, and the pull that follows is a performance of force rather than an application of it.

Then the movement resolves. Saberist A completes twice on the 9 line while Saberist B dodges both, and the exchange ends with the two Saberists apart rather than bound — which is only legible as a resolution because so much of what came before was spent locked together.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-G is designed to teach:

  • locks as the structure of a movement rather than as a single milestone
  • X, and S+S for a lock that is held
  • entering a lock from a parry, and from an attack that is met
  • carrying a parry from one line to another, as in 3P>9PX
  • pulling against a stand-off safely and convincingly
  • answering a complete with movement instead of a blade
  • pacing a long exchange with deliberate stops

docs.title: Phase 1: Static walkthrough
docs.text:
Take the eleven steps one at a time, standing, at no speed at all.

Walk into each lock and stop there. Confirm before moving on:

  • both Saberists arrive at the lock at the same moment
  • the blades meet at an agreed angle and height
  • distance is safe, with room for both Saberists to pull
  • the release is agreed before it happens

docs.title: Phase 2: The locks on their own
docs.text:
Practise the three locks as isolated pairs of steps, out of sequence.

The opening stand-off needs the most work, because it is the only one that is held. Set the thrust, the 3P>9PX parry into the lock, and the two pulls as a single unit, and repeat it until entry, hold and release are the same every time.

docs.title: Phase 3: The runs between the locks
docs.text:
Now practise the blade work on its own: steps 4 and 5, steps 7 and 8, steps 10 and 11.

These are the parts of the movement that travel, and they are short by design. Run each one until it is clean before joining it to anything.

docs.title: Phase 4: Slow continuous flow
docs.text:
Put the whole eleven steps together, slowly, without stopping.

The seams are the transitions in and out of each lock. If either Saberist loses the sequence, stop and restart from step 1 rather than picking it up mid-lock.

docs.title: Phase 5: Performance pace
docs.text:
Only once the sequence is reliable, add speed to the runs — and leave the locks alone.

A lock does not get faster. It gets longer. Bringing the exchange up to performance pace means the blade work quickens while the held moments stay held, and the difference between the two is what an audience actually sees.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-G should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

The hazard that belongs to this movement is close quarters. Every lock brings two Saberists within a blade's length of each other with weapons engaged, and CM-G does that three times in eleven steps. Locks are entered slowly and by agreement, always — and a pair that is comfortable with the sequence is exactly the pair most likely to start arriving at the lock a little faster than they agreed.

It is also worth naming what the film reference is and is not. CM-G is an interpretation of a filmed duel, worked out and written down by Saberists. Learning it teaches the notation, not a reconstruction of anyone's performance.

When CM-G is clean, continue to CM-H, which trades the stops for continuous flow, or return to the Extended Library.

docs.title: CM-H
docs.text:
CM-H is six hits that cross the body in a zig-zag, run without stopping.

It is one of the shortest movements in the Extended Library and one of the easiest to keep going, which is exactly the point. Once the six hits are automatic, a pair has a reliable phrase they can carry into longer choreography and build improvisation around.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 Saberist A 2 10 3 8 5 11 Saberist B 2P 10P 3P 8P 5P 11X

This is the plainest table in the Extended Library, and reading it takes three observations.

  • Saberist B answers each attack with the parry of the same number. 2 is met with 2P, 10 with 10P, and so on. Nothing in the first five steps asks either Saberist to do anything but attack and parry.
  • Every strike crosses to the other side of the body from the one before it. 2 to 10, 3 to 8, 5 to 11 — high right to high left, middle right to low left, low right to high left. That alternation is the zig-zag the movement is named for.
  • The last step is a lock, not a parry. Saberist A's 11 is not turned aside; 11X catches it, and the movement holds there. X is the lock introduced in CM-E.

docs.title: Telegraph
docs.text:
Both hands holding the saber hilt horizontally.

The telegraph is the silent signal that calls CM-H before an exchange begins. See LUMINA Games for how telegraphs are used in play.

docs.title: Continuous flow
docs.text:
Flow is what happens when the recovery from one strike is already the preparation for the next.

A sequence learned step by step tends to be performed step by step: strike, return to guard, strike, return to guard. That is the right way to learn it and the wrong way to perform it. Every return to guard is a moment where nothing is happening, and a fight assembled from them looks like a list of attacks rather than a fight.

CM-H is built to remove those gaps, and the zig-zag is how it does it. Because each strike finishes on the opposite side of the body from where the next one starts, the blade is already travelling in roughly the right direction when the previous hit ends. There is nothing to undo. The end of 2 is most of the way to the start of 10; the end of 10 is on the way to 3. Run in order, the six hits describe one continuous path across the body rather than six separate journeys out from the middle.

That is why the movement is short. Six hits is enough to feel the path and not so many that a Saberist has to think about which comes next — and thinking about which comes next is the other thing that puts gaps in a sequence.

Saberist B has the same problem in mirror image. Five parries in a row, alternating sides, have to be found without resetting between them, which means the parry is taken where the attack is going rather than where the last parry left the blade. A defender who returns to a neutral guard after every parry will always be a beat behind on the next one.

The lock at the end is the movement's full stop. Five exchanges run continuously and then stop dead, held, on the sixth. Coming to a genuine standstill after continuous motion is harder than it sounds and is worth practising as its own skill: the flow has to end on a decision, not run out of momentum.

Because the phrase is short, self-contained, and ends somewhere definite, CM-H is a natural place to improvise around. Vary the tempo, vary the footwork, vary what happens after the lock. Do not vary the six hits themselves — the sequence is the fixed thing that lets everything around it move.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-H is designed to teach:

  • continuous motion through a sequence, with no reset between strikes
  • a zig-zag attack path that alternates across the body
  • attacking and parrying on alternating sides without returning to guard
  • six-hit phrasing as a unit that can be dropped into longer choreography
  • ending continuous motion on a deliberate stop
  • X as a lock that closes a movement
  • a fixed phrase as a foundation for improvisation

docs.title: Phase 1: Static walkthrough
docs.text:
Take the six hits one at a time, standing, with a full stop after each.

Confirm at every step:

  • both Saberists agree which target the number names
  • the parry meets the attack cleanly
  • distance is safe
  • the step can be repeated the same way

Do not attempt to connect anything yet. The zig-zag has to be correct before it can be smooth.

docs.title: Phase 2: Pairs
docs.text:
Join the hits two at a time — steps 1 and 2, then 2 and 3, then 3 and 4, and so on.

Each pair is where a crossing happens, and each one is a small problem of its own: how does the blade get from the end of the first hit to the start of the second without going back to the middle? Solve them individually.

docs.title: Phase 3: Slow continuous flow
docs.text:
Run all six hits at low speed without a stop anywhere in them.

Speed is not the goal here and will make the gaps harder to see. Run it slowly enough that both Saberists can feel exactly where the blade pauses, then work on that seam.

docs.title: Phase 4: The lock
docs.text:
Add the lock at step 6 last.

Practise arriving at it out of continuous motion, which is the part that needs work — a lock entered while still travelling is the one place this movement can get careless. Enter it slowly and by agreement, as always, and only bring the preceding five hits up to speed once the stop is reliable.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-H should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

The hazard that belongs to this movement is its own smoothness. Continuous motion invites speed, and CM-H is easy enough that a pair reaches the point of running it comfortably long before they have earned the right to run it quickly. Six hits with no stops in them leave no moment to correct a mistake, so pace is added only when the path is identical every repetition.

It is also the first movement where a Saberist is asked to make a sequence look like one action rather than six. That is a performance skill as much as a technical one, and it is the reason CM-H sits where it does in the library.

When CM-H is clean, continue to CM-I, which takes the same idea into completes, or return to the Extended Library.

docs.title: CM-I
docs.text:
CM-I is a nine-strike sequence built around completes, and it carries a piece of the history of saber choreography with it.
