Matthew Carauddo developed the Novastar Caine Saber Combat System in the early days of LED stunt sabering and taught it through a series of instructional videos released as Saber Combat. SaberCraft's founder trained this sequence with him at a clinic. Saber Combat is no longer available, so the sequence is written down here for posterity — an example of one of the earliest saber strike sequences developed by a fan, for fans.

CM-I is based on choreography by Matthew Carauddo for Saber Combat, applied to the CM structure. To learn more about Saber Combat, visit SaberCombat.com.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
Wide tables

The table below is wide. On a phone, turn the device landscape; the table can also be scrolled sideways.

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 s9 Saberist A 5 9 2© 1 3 7 3© 7© 11 Saberist B 5P 9P 2P 1P 3P 7P 3P 7P 11P
  • Saberist B answers every attack with the parry of the same number. 5 is met with 5P, 9 with 9P, and so on to the end of the sequence. Saberist A carries the whole movement.
  • © is a complete, taught in CM-C. The swing carries through the target instead of stopping at it, and finishes somewhere the blade would not have reached otherwise.
  • Three of the nine strikes complete: 2© at step 3, then 3© and 7© back to back at steps 7 and 8. The other six stop.
  • Steps 5 and 6 return as steps 7 and 8. 3 and 7 are struck twice — the first time stopping, the second time completing. Same lines, different endings.

docs.title: Telegraph
docs.text:
A vertical front propellor flourish.

The telegraph is the silent signal that calls CM-I before an exchange begins. See LUMINA Games for how telegraphs are used in play.

docs.title: Advanced completes
docs.text:
CM-C introduces the complete as an idea: some swings stop at the target, and some carry through. CM-I is where that idea has to do real work.

A stopping strike ends where it lands. The blade arrives, it is met, and it is then somewhere known — which means the next strike starts from a known place, and a sequence of stopping strikes is a sequence of separate decisions. A complete does not offer that. It passes through the target and keeps travelling, and it ends wherever its arc takes it. What follows a complete is therefore not chosen freely; it is chosen from where the blade actually is.

That is the whole difficulty of this movement, and it is arranged in ascending order.

The first complete stands alone. 2© at step 3 sits between two stopping strikes, so a Saberist can carry it through and then re-set before 1 at step 4. It is a complete with a safety net, and it is the one to learn first.

The two at steps 7 and 8 have no such net. 3© runs straight into 7©, which means the second complete starts from wherever the first one finished, with no stop in between to recover from. Two carried swings in a row is a different skill from one, and it is the reason CM-I is called advanced rather than simply another sequence of completes. Get the arc of 3© wrong and 7© is not merely late — it starts from the wrong place entirely.

The repetition is what teaches it. Steps 5 and 6 strike the 3 and 7 lines and stop; steps 7 and 8 strike the same two lines and carry through. Running them back to back makes the difference impossible to miss, and it is worth practising the four steps as a block for exactly that reason. The same two lines, twice, ending differently — that comparison is the lesson.

Saberist B has the harder half of it. Parrying a stopping strike and parrying a completing one are not the same action: a complete keeps moving after contact, so the parry has to deflect and then get clear rather than hold position. A defender who meets 3© the way they met 3 will find the blade still travelling through where they are standing. Both Saberists must know which strikes complete, before the sequence starts, every time.

Nine strikes, six that stop and three that carry, is a small enough sequence to hold in the head and a demanding enough one to take a long time to make clean. That combination is why it has outlived the videos it came from.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-I is designed to teach:

  • completes inside a long sequence rather than as an isolated technique
  • two completes run back to back, with no reset between them
  • choosing the next strike from where a carried swing actually ends
  • the difference between striking a line and completing through it
  • parrying a complete, which deflects and clears rather than holds
  • nine-strike phrasing held as a single movement

docs.title: Phase 1: Static walkthrough
docs.text:
Take the nine strikes one at a time, standing, with a full stop after each.

Perform every strike as a stopping strike for now, completes included. Confirm at each step:

  • both Saberists agree which target the number names
  • the parry meets the attack cleanly
  • distance is safe
  • the step can be repeated the same way

docs.title: Phase 2: One complete at a time
docs.text:
Add 2© at step 3 and nothing else.

Run steps 1 to 4 until the complete carries through cleanly, Saberist B's parry clears it, and step 4 starts from wherever the blade has ended up. Only then move on.

docs.title: Phase 3: The pair at steps 7 and 8
docs.text:
Practise steps 5 through 8 as a block, out of sequence.

This is the heart of the movement. Run 3 and 7 stopping, then 3© and 7© completing, and pay attention to where the second complete begins. If 7© feels rushed, the problem is almost always the arc of 3© before it, not the strike itself.

docs.title: Phase 4: Slow continuous flow
docs.text:
Put all nine strikes together at low speed, without stopping.

If either Saberist loses the sequence, restart from step 1 rather than picking it up mid-complete.

docs.title: Phase 5: Performance pace
docs.text:
Add speed only once the completes are identical every repetition.

A complete run fast by a Saberist who is not certain where it ends is the least controlled thing in this movement. Certainty first, then pace.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-I should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

The hazard that belongs to this movement is the carried swing. A complete does not stop at the target, so the distance that is safe for a stopping strike is not automatically safe here — and steps 7 and 8 put two of them in a row. Set the working distance for the completes, not for the sequence's shortest strike, and check it again whenever the pace changes.

There is also something worth telling students about why this movement is in the library at all. CM-I is not an interpretation of a filmed fight, and it is not original to the Saber Standard. It is an early piece of community choreography, taught in person, recorded on discs that are no longer sold, and preserved here because notation is how a movement survives the medium it was taught in. That is a reasonable answer to the question of what the notation is for.

When CM-I is clean, continue to CM-J, which turns the saber around, or return to the Extended Library.

docs.title: CM-J
docs.text:
CM-J turns the saber around. Saberist A works the movement in an inverted grip — the hilt held so the blade runs down from the fist rather than up from it — and every attack, parry and spin in the sequence is shaped by that one change.

The choreography around the grip is deliberately plain. Eleven steps, no locks, no completes, and a parry answering every attack. Nothing competes with the thing being learned.

Saberist B has a choice. Answering in a standard grip keeps the contrast visible and makes the movement easy to read from outside. Taking the inverted grip as well turns CM-J into an exchange fought entirely reversed, which is harder and considerably more striking to watch.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
Wide tables

The table below is wide. On a phone, turn the device landscape; the table can also be scrolled sideways.

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 s9 s10 s11 Saberist A Ig 3P Ig11 Ig1 Ig7 Ig3-Spin Ig 3P 5 9 3 7 11 Saberist B 3 11P 1P 7P 3P-Spin 3 5P 9P 3P 7P 11P

Read down each column as usual. The eleven steps fall into two halves.

  • Ig is the inverted grip, listed in the Notation Legend. It is written on Saberist A's cells through the first six steps, and the lesson describes the whole movement as Saberist A's inverted-grip drill.
  • Steps 1 and 6 are Saberist B's. B strikes 3 and Saberist A takes it on an inverted-grip parry, Ig 3P. The same exchange opens the movement and closes its first half.
  • Steps 2 to 5 are Saberist A's, and B answers each with the parry of the same number: Ig11 against 11P, Ig1 against 1P, Ig7 against 7P.
  • Step 5 is shared. Ig3-Spin and 3P-Spin are the same beat — both Saberists spin, one attacking on the 3 line and one parrying it.
  • Steps 7 to 11 are a straight run. Saberist A attacks 5, 9, 3, 7, 11 and Saberist B parries each in turn. No spins, no grip marks — the second half is written plain, and it is where the sequence picks up speed.

docs.title: Telegraph
docs.text:
A forward flourish performed in the inverted grip — Ig-Fl-Fwd.

The telegraph is the silent signal that calls CM-J before an exchange begins. See LUMINA Games for how telegraphs are used in play.

docs.title: The inverted grip
docs.text:
Every movement up to this point assumes the blade leaves the hand in one direction. CM-J removes that assumption.

Turn the hilt over and the blade now extends downward from the fist. Nothing about the target lines changes — a 1 is still a 1-o'clock attack, an 11P is still a parry on the 11 line — but almost everything about how the arm reaches them does. Attacks that were natural are now awkward, and attacks that were awkward become surprisingly direct. That inversion is the entire lesson, and it is why the sequence is short enough to memorize in a few minutes and long enough to take weeks to make clean.

Three things change immediately.

The first is where the blade sits at rest. In a standard grip the blade is out in front, between the two Saberists, and it is visible at all times. Inverted, it hangs down and back along the forearm, which means a Saberist who is used to seeing their own blade in the corner of their eye no longer does. The blade has to be known rather than watched.

The second is the parry. Ig 3P opens the movement, and it is the first thing to practise, because an inverted parry is not a standard parry with the wrist turned over. The blade meets the attack from the other side, and the structure holding it there is the forearm rather than the wrist. Get that structure right and the parry is solid; get it wrong and it collapses on contact.

The third is the spin at step 5. Both Saberists turn on the same beat, one striking the 3 line and one parrying it, and the Saberist in the inverted grip is turning a blade that trails behind the hand. A spin that is comfortable in a standard grip needs re-learning from the beginning here — which is exactly why it sits at the midpoint, with five steps before it to settle into the grip and five after it to recover.

Then the second half opens out. Steps 7 to 11 are five attacks and five parries with nothing else in them: 5, 9, 3, 7, 11. After the constraint of the first half, that run is where a Saberist finds out whether the grip has actually become comfortable or has merely been survived one step at a time.

If both Saberists take the inverted grip, the movement changes character rather than difficulty. The parries meet at unfamiliar angles, the whole exchange sits lower, and the pair should expect to reset their working distance before running it that way.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-J is designed to teach:

  • the inverted grip, noted Ig, as a working grip rather than a flourish
  • attacking on familiar target lines from an unfamiliar hand position
  • the inverted parry, and the forearm structure that holds it
  • spinning with a blade that trails behind the hand
  • knowing where the blade is without being able to see it
  • reading an opponent whose blade is reversed

docs.title: Phase 1: The grip alone
docs.text:
Take the grip with no partner and no sequence.

Turn the hilt over and simply move: hold the blade still, swing slowly along each of the six beginner lines, and return. Do this until the grip stops feeling like a trick and starts feeling like a position. Nothing in CM-J is worth attempting before that happens.

docs.title: Phase 2: The parry
docs.text:
Practise Ig 3P on its own, statically, with a partner striking 3 slowly.

This is the movement's foundation, and it is worth more repetitions than anything else on the page. Confirm at every repetition:

  • the blade meets the attack rather than being pushed by it
  • the forearm, not the wrist, is holding the structure
  • distance is safe
  • the parry can be repeated the same way

docs.title: Phase 3: Steps 1 to 6 statically
docs.text:
Walk the first half one step at a time, with a full stop after each.

Add nothing to it yet, including the spin — perform step 5 as a plain 3 and 3P for now. The point of this phase is that Saberist A finds each target line from the inverted grip without hunting for it.

docs.title: Phase 4: The spin
docs.text:
Add step 5 as written, out of sequence.

Both Saberists turn together, so agree the direction and the timing before either of them moves. Practise it as a single beat, repeated, until the turn and the strike arrive at the same moment. Only then put it back into the first half.

docs.title: Phase 5: The second half
docs.text:
Run steps 7 to 11 on their own.

Five attacks, five parries, in order, at low speed. This half has no complications in it by design, so it is the place to work on the flow of the grip rather than its mechanics.

docs.title: Phase 6: The whole sequence
docs.text:
Join both halves, slowly, and add speed only when the grip is reliable.

If Saberist B is also working inverted, run the whole movement once more from Phase 3 with that change in place. It is a different sequence in the hands, even though nothing on the page has changed.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-J should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

The hazard that belongs to this movement is the part of the blade a Saberist cannot see. Inverted, the blade hangs behind and below the hand, which puts it near the Saberist's own legs and near the floor, and puts the tip somewhere neither Saberist is looking. Give the pair more room than the sequence appears to need, and check the space behind and below before every repetition rather than once at the start.

It is also worth telling students why a grip gets a movement of its own. The notation does not change here — the target lines, the parries and the spin are all written exactly as they would be in a standard grip. What changes is the body performing them. CM-J is the clearest demonstration in the library that the notation describes what happens between two Saberists, not how any one of them holds a hilt.

When CM-J is clean, continue to CM-K, which brings a staff into the exchange, or return to the Extended Library.

docs.title: CM-K
docs.text:
CM-K brings a second weapon into the Saber Standard. Saberist A carries a saber; Saberist B carries a staff, and the movement is written for that mismatch rather than around it.

It interprets the first half of the duel between Obi-Wan Kenobi and Darth Maul in Star Wars: The Phantom Menace. CM-L continues the same fight.

CM-K was notated by Armando Valdivia and Alfred Smith.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
CM-K is written in five short tables, read in order.

Wide tables

The tables below are wide. On a phone, turn the device landscape; any of them can also be scrolled sideways.

Part 1

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 Saberist A 1 5 7X 1P Duck Saberist B L1P R5P Spin R>L L7PX X-O R1 L10©

Part 2

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 Saberist A 3P - Back 1 5 7X 1P Saberist B L3 L1P R5P Spin R>L L7PX X-O R1

Part 3

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 Saberist A Duck 3P - Back 9PX 11P 5P 12P Saberist B L10© L3 R9X L11B Spin R>L L5 R12

Part 4

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 Saberist A 11P 4P Duck 3P 8P 4P Spin L > R Saberist B R12 L11 R4 J10© L3 Back R8 L4

Part 5

Player s1 s2 Saberist A 7© 9© Saberist B 3©

Read down each column as usual. Saberist B's row is the one that reads differently from every other movement in the library.

  • Every cell in Saberist B's row begins with L or R. That letter is the hand that strikes with the staff — L for the left hand, R for the right. Hand positions on the staff are the Saberist's own choice; the lesson recommends the right palm facing down and the left palm facing up.
  • The hands alternate almost every beat. L1P, R5P, then L7PX, then R1 — the staff turns end over end through the exchange, and which hand drives each strike is as much a part of the notation as the target number.
  • X is a lock, from CM-E. It appears in both rows at the same step: 7X against L7PX in Parts 1 and 2, and 9PX against R9X in Part 3.
  • B is a bash and J is a jump, both in the Notation Legend. L11B in Part 3 is a left-handed bash on the 11 line; J10© in Part 4 is a jumping complete on the 10 line, which is the attack Saberist A ducks.
  • © is a complete, taught in CM-C. The swing carries through rather than stopping — which is why Saberist A answers L10© with a Duck rather than a parry.
  • X-O follows the lock. In both openings it sits between L7PX and Saberist B's next strike, on a beat where nothing is written for Saberist A. The demonstration video shows what happens there.
  • A blank cell means nothing is written for that Saberist on that beat. They hold while the other acts.
  • Parts 1 and 2 are the same phrase. Part 2 opens with Saberist A stepping back on a 3 parry against L3, and then repeats 1, 5, the spin, 7X, X-O and 1P exactly as Part 1 wrote them, one step later in the count. Part 3 opens on the two beats that closed Part 1 and opened Part 2 — Duck against L10©, then 3P - Back against L3 — before the movement turns into new material at 9PX.
  • R12 closes Part 3 and opens Part 4, where Saberist A's cell is left empty. Saberist A's 12P against it is written once, at the end of Part 3.

docs.title: Telegraph
docs.text:
Saberist A: two fingers pointed at the opponent, then down. Saberist B: the staff pointed down in front of you, at the 5 position.

Both halves are given, one for each Saberist — A signals with the hand, B with the staff.

The telegraph is the silent signal that calls CM-K before an exchange begins. See LUMINA Games for how telegraphs are used in play.

docs.title: The staff
docs.text:
Everything before CM-K is written for two Saberists holding the same kind of weapon. Both rows of every table describe the same instrument, so a 5 in one row and a 5P in the other are two versions of one action. The staff breaks that symmetry, and the notation has to carry the difference.

It carries it with a single letter. L or R in front of every one of Saberist B's cells says which hand is driving the strike, and that is the whole of the extra vocabulary CM-K needs. The target numbers are unchanged. The parries are unchanged. What is new is that the weapon has two working ends, and the notation has to say which one is coming.

That is more information than it first appears to be. A saber strike is one blade travelling one path, and a defender who knows the number knows where it is going. A staff strike is one end of a long weapon rotating around two hands, and the other end is going somewhere too. Reading R5P means reading not only the 5 line but which end of the staff is answering on it — and therefore where the far end has swung to, and what it is in position to do next.

For Saberist B the lesson is the alternation. Look down the row: L1P, R5P, L7PX, R1, L10©. The hands trade almost every beat, and each trade turns the staff over. Performed well, that is a weapon in continuous rotation with a strike falling out of it at each half-turn; performed badly, it is a series of separate swings with the staff hauled back into position between them. The recommended hand positions — right palm down, left palm up — exist to make the turn possible without regripping, and they are worth setting before any of the sequence is attempted.

For Saberist A the lesson is reach. A staff is longer than a saber, and it is longer at both ends, so the distance at which Saberist A is safe is not the distance CM-A through CM-J have trained. Notice how much of Saberist A's row is not blade work at all: Duck twice, 3P - Back twice, a jump-height complete to avoid in Part 4. Against a staff, moving out of the way is not a fallback for when the parry is unavailable. It is a primary answer, and it is used here as often as the parry is.

The two locks are where the mismatch is most visible. 7X against L7PX in Parts 1 and 2, and 9PX against R9X in Part 3, each bind a saber to a staff — and a staff in a lock still has a free end, held by the other hand, at a completely different distance. Locks with a staff are entered slowly, at an agreed angle, with both Saberists clear on where the far end has gone.

The repetition in Parts 1 and 2 is the movement's way of teaching all of this. The same six beats are run twice, separated only by Saberist A stepping back on 3P - Back, and Part 3 begins by running the seam a third time before it moves on. That is deliberate: the phrase is short, it contains a spin, a lock and a complete, and running it twice before the fight develops gives both Saberists the pattern in their hands before the choreography asks anything new of them.

Part 5 ends the movement with three completes. Saberist A carries through on 7© and 9©, Saberist B answers the second with 3©, and the exchange finishes with both weapons still travelling rather than stopped or bound.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-K is designed to teach:

  • choreography between two different weapons rather than two of the same
  • L and R as the hand that strikes with the staff
  • alternating hands so the staff turns over continuously between strikes
  • reading a weapon with two working ends
  • working at staff distance, where evasion is a primary answer rather than a fallback
  • locking a saber against a staff safely
  • holding a short phrase steady through repetition before the fight develops

docs.title: Phase 1: The staff alone
docs.text:
Saberist B works the staff with no partner and no sequence.

Set the hand positions first — right palm down, left palm up is the recommendation — and then simply turn the staff over, left hand to right hand and back, slowly, until the rotation happens without regripping. Learn where the far end is at every point in that turn. Everything else in CM-K depends on this.

docs.title: Phase 2: Distance
docs.text:
Stand the pair at the distance the staff actually needs and check it before anything is performed.

Saberist A should find the range at which the staff can reach them and the range at which it cannot, from both ends, and Saberist B should confirm both. This phase produces a working distance, not a sequence.

docs.title: Phase 3: Part 1 statically
docs.text:
Walk the seven steps of Part 1 one at a time, with a full stop after each.

Confirm at every step:

  • both Saberists agree which target the number names
  • Saberist B's striking hand is the one the cell names
  • the parry, duck or lock meets the attack cleanly
  • distance is safe for the whole staff, not just the striking end
  • the step can be repeated the same way

docs.title: Phase 4: The lock and the spin
docs.text:
Practise 7X against L7PX, and Saberist B's Spin R>L, as isolated beats.

These are the two places in the phrase where the staff's far end moves furthest from where Saberist A is looking. Enter the lock slowly and by agreement, every time, and agree the direction of the spin before either Saberist moves.

docs.title: Phase 5: Parts 1 and 2 together
docs.text:
Run the repeated phrase twice through, joined by 3P - Back.

This is the movement's spine. It should be reliable, at low speed, before Part 3 is introduced — the repetition exists so that the pattern is automatic by the time the choreography develops.

docs.title: Phase 6: Parts 3 and 4
docs.text:
Add the new material a part at a time.

Part 3 brings the bash and the second lock; Part 4 brings the jumping complete and the longest run of continuous staff attack in the movement. Work each on its own before joining it to what comes before.

docs.title: Phase 7: The finish, then pace
docs.text:
Add Part 5 last, then bring the whole movement up to speed.

The three completes at the end travel further than anything else in CM-K, so they are set at the distance the completes need. Speed is added to the runs of blade work only, and never to the locks.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-K should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

The hazard that belongs to this movement is the end of the staff nobody is watching. A saber has one dangerous end and it is the one both Saberists are looking at. A staff has two, and the far one moves fastest exactly when the near one is doing something interesting — during a spin, during a lock, during a bash. Every phase above is run at a distance that accounts for the whole weapon, and a pair that has grown comfortable with the sequence is the pair most likely to let that distance close.

It is also worth naming what a second weapon means for the notation. Nothing in CM-K required a new system. A single letter in front of the target number was enough to carry a different weapon through an entire movement, because the notation describes what happens between two Saberists rather than what either one is holding. That is the argument for writing choreography down in the first place, and CM-K is the clearest example of it in the library.

When CM-K is clean, continue to CM-L, which carries the same duel into its second half, or return to the Extended Library.

docs.title: CM-L
docs.text:
CM-L is the second half of the staff duel begun in CM-K. Saberist A carries a saber, Saberist B carries the staff, and the same lesson video carries both movements.

Where CM-K trades initiative back and forth, CM-L does not. Saberist B attacks from the first beat to the last, and Saberist A answers all sixteen steps without a single attack of their own. It is the longest unbroken defence in the Extended Library, and that is what it is for.

Like CM-K, it interprets the duel between Obi-Wan Kenobi and Darth Maul in Star Wars: The Phantom Menace, and it was notated by Armando Valdivia and Alfred Smith.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
CM-L runs sixteen steps, written in two tables.

Wide tables

Both tables below are wide. On a phone, turn the device landscape; either table can also be scrolled sideways.

The opening

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 Saberist A 9P 5P Jump 3P 1P 11P Saberist B Fl:P L-R R9 L5 R7© (x2) L3 R1 L11

The run

Player s8 s9 s10 s11 s12 s13 s14 s15 s16 Saberist A 4P 8P 1P 3P Back 9PX L1P R5P 12P Saberist B R4 L8 R1 L3 R9X 1 5 12 Kick

Read down each column as usual, and notice what is missing: there is no attack anywhere in Saberist A's row.

  • Saberist B carries the whole movement. Every step is a staff attack, and Saberist A answers each one with a parry, a jump, a step back or a lock.
  • L and R name the striking hand, as in CM-K — the staff turns over between strikes, and the letter says which end is coming. The hands alternate almost every beat: R9, L5, R7©, L3, R1, L11.
  • Fl:P is the vertical front propellor flourish, listed as Fl-P in the Notation Legend. Saberist B opens the movement with it while Saberist A does nothing at all.
  • R7© (x2) is struck twice. It is a completing 7 — a low line, carried through rather than stopped, delivered right-handed and repeated — and Saberist A's answer to both is Jump.
  • © is a complete, taught in CM-C; X is a lock, from CM-E. The single lock is at step 12, where 9PX meets R9X.
  • Steps 13 and 14 are written differently. Saberist B's 1 and 5 carry no hand mark, and Saberist A's parries carry L and R instead. That is how the source lesson writes them; the demonstration video shows the beat.
  • The movement ends on a kick. Kick at step 16 is Saberist B's only unarmed action, and nothing is written for Saberist A against it.

docs.title: Holding a long defence
docs.text:
A defence in the Core Library lasts one exchange. An attack arrives, it is parried, and the roles change over — CM-D is built on exactly that switch. CM-L removes the switch and asks what happens when it never comes.

Sixteen attacks arrive in a row. Saberist A parries fourteen of them, jumps one, and finishes standing still while a kick lands. There is no point at which the defending Saberist gets to answer, and no point at which the pressure lets up, and that is the entire subject of the movement.

Three things make a long defence different from a short one, and all three are visible in the notation.

The first is that the parries stop being separate decisions. Look at steps 8 to 11: 4P, 8P, 1P, 3P Back. Four lines in four beats, high to low and back, with nothing between them. A Saberist who takes each parry, recovers to guard, and then looks for the next one will be late on the second and lost by the fourth. Each parry has to be taken from wherever the last one finished, in the direction the next attack is already coming from. That is the same continuous-motion skill CM-H teaches on the attacking side, arriving here on the defending side and under far more pressure.

The second is that the defence has to travel. 3P Back at step 11 is the only cell in Saberist A's row that names footwork, and it is placed exactly where the sequence needs it — a parry taken while giving ground, resetting the distance before the lock at step 12. A long defence that stays rooted runs out of room, because a staff at full extension will always find the range eventually. Giving ground at the right moment is a defensive action in its own right, and CM-L writes it into the middle of the phrase rather than leaving it to instinct.

The third is that not everything can be parried. Step 4 is a completing 7 struck twice — a low line, carried through, and coming back. Saberist A's answer is Jump, because a blade in the way of a carried low sweep is not a defence, it is a collision. Against a staff, choosing between the parry and the evasion is part of reading the attack, and this movement puts the choice in the middle of the opening phrase where it cannot be avoided.

Then there is the lock at step 12, and it is the only moment in sixteen steps where the attack stops. 9PX against R9X binds the saber to the staff, holds, and gives both Saberists a beat of stillness in the middle of a continuous assault. In performance that is where an audience catches up. In training it is where the defending Saberist finds out whether they have been breathing.

What follows the lock is the fastest part of the movement — 1, 5, 12 in three beats, straight into the kick — and it works because the lock came first. A run of attacks after a held moment reads as an escalation. The same run without it would read as more of the same.

The kick is the finish. Saberist B's only unarmed action in the movement ends it, and nothing is written for Saberist A in reply. A defence that has held for sixteen steps against the weapon is ended by something that is not the weapon at all, and that is the point the sequence is making.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-L is designed to teach:

  • sustained defence across a long phrase with no change of roles
  • taking each parry from where the last one finished, without returning to guard
  • choosing between a parry and an evasion as the attack demands
  • giving ground deliberately, as a defensive action rather than a retreat
  • answering a repeated, completing low attack with a jump
  • a lock used as the single rest in a continuous assault
  • an unarmed finish against an armed opponent

docs.title: Phase 1: The opening statically
docs.text:
Walk steps 1 to 7 one at a time, with a full stop after each.

Confirm at every step:

  • both Saberists agree which target the number names
  • Saberist B's striking hand is the one the cell names
  • the parry meets the attack cleanly, and at a distance safe for the whole staff
  • the step can be repeated the same way

Perform step 4 as a single stopping strike for now, parried rather than jumped. The jump is added later.

docs.title: Phase 2: The jump at step 4
docs.text:
Practise R7© (x2) and Jump as an isolated pair of beats.

This is the most dangerous beat in the movement and it deserves its own session. Set the height of the sweep, the timing of the jump, and the second repetition, slowly and by agreement, and repeat it until the two Saberists arrive together every time. Speed is added last, and only here.

docs.title: Phase 3: The run statically
docs.text:
Walk steps 8 to 16 the same way, one at a time.

The four parries at steps 8 to 11 are the block to concentrate on. Take them in order and pay attention to where each parry finishes rather than to where it starts — that is what makes the next one reachable.

docs.title: Phase 4: The lock and the finish
docs.text:
Practise step 12 on its own, then steps 13 to 16 as a run.

Enter the lock slowly and by agreement, as always, and remember that the far end of the staff is still free while the near end is bound. Then set the kick: agreed target, agreed distance, no contact, exactly the same every repetition.

docs.title: Phase 5: Slow continuous flow
docs.text:
Put all sixteen steps together at low speed, without stopping.

The seams are the entry to the jump, the entry to the lock, and the exit from it. If either Saberist loses the sequence, restart from step 1 rather than picking it up mid-phrase.

docs.title: Phase 6: Performance pace
docs.text:
Add speed to the runs of parries, and leave the jump, the lock and the kick where they are.

CM-L should accelerate after the lock and not before it. That shape is the difference between a long defence that builds and a long defence that simply continues.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-L should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

Two hazards belong to this movement. The first is fatigue: sixteen attacks in a row is genuinely tiring for both Saberists, and a tired parry is a late parry. Run it in halves for longer than seems necessary, and stop the moment either Saberist's timing starts to drift — the last thing a pair should practise is what this sequence looks like when they are too tired to perform it. The second is the low sweep at step 4, which is struck twice, carries through, and is answered by leaving the ground. Nothing else in the Extended Library asks a Saberist to jump a completing attack, and it is set at an agreed height, at an agreed speed, before it is ever run in sequence.

It is also worth telling students what a movement without a single attack in one row is doing in a notation system. CM-F wrote a full sequence for a Saberist with no weapon; CM-L writes one for a Saberist who never attacks. Both are complete movements, both are written in the same language, and neither needs a special case to be read. A row of parries, jumps and ground given up is notation in exactly the same sense as a row of strikes.

When CM-L is clean, continue to CM-M, which inverts the direction of the exchange, or return to the Extended Library.

docs.title: CM-M
docs.text:
CM-M is built on constant attack, answer, and reversal of direction. It interprets a duel between Count Dooku and Anakin Skywalker, from a deleted scene of Star Wars: Episode III — Revenge of the Sith.

Everything in the library up to this point answers an attack by giving ground. The defending Saberist parries, ducks or steps back, and the exchange travels away from the attack. CM-M turns that around: the Saberist under attack advances, closes the distance, and the defence becomes forward pressure. It is the first movement in which the direction of the exchange is fully inverted.

CM-M was notated by Rhamses Nazario and Enrique Santana.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
CM-M runs seventeen steps, written in two tables.

Wide tables

Both tables below are wide. On a phone, turn the device landscape; either table can also be scrolled sideways.

The opening

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 s9 s10 Saberist A (Anakin) 7P S-CCW D J + S-CCW 4 12 3Pm6 S-CW Saberist B (Dooku) 7 S-CCW 2© 5© 4P 12P Re S-CCW 3

The run

Player s11 s12 s13 s14 s15 s16 s17 Saberist A (Anakin) 3Pm6x x 1B 11B 12P Re Special Saberist B (Dooku) 9x x 1B 11B 12

Read down each column as usual. What is unusual here is how often the two rows carry the same cell.

  • Initiative changes hands twice. Saberist B attacks through steps 1 to 4, Saberist A attacks at steps 5 and 6, and Saberist B attacks again at step 9. Neither Saberist holds the attack for long, which is what gives the movement its back-and-forth shape.
  • S-CCW and S-CW are spins, counter clockwise and clockwise, listed as S CCW and S CW in the Notation Legend. There are four of them, and both Saberists spin together at step 2.
  • © is a complete, taught in CM-C. Saberist B's 2© and 5© carry through rather than stopping, and Saberist A answers them with D — a duck — and then J + S-CCW, a jump into a counter-clockwise spin.
  • 3Pm6 is a parry with a modifier. It is a 3 parry taken with the tip pointing down at 6, the example the Notation Legend gives for M. Saberist A uses it twice, at steps 9 and 11.
  • Re is a recoil, a bounce back off the parry. Saberist B recoils at step 7 and Saberist A at step 16, in both cases immediately after their attack has been answered.
  • x holds into the next move. At step 11 both Saberists write it — 3Pm6x against 9x — and at step 12 both rows carry x alone. The blades stay bound across two beats before the movement continues.
  • Steps 13 and 14 are identical in both rows. 1B and then 11B are bashes struck by both Saberists on the same beat, on the same line.
  • Special closes the movement. As in CM-E, the notation names the slot and the Saberists performing it choose what fills it.
  • A blank cell means nothing is written for that Saberist on that beat. They hold while the other acts.

docs.title: Telegraph
docs.text:
Both Saberists point their saber tips down at 45°. Saberist B holds at shoulder level; Saberist A at mid-section level.

The telegraph is the silent signal that calls CM-M before an exchange begins. See LUMINA Games for how telegraphs are used in play.

docs.title: Inverting the exchange
docs.text:
A movement has a direction. In CM-A the attacker comes forward and the defender holds or gives way; in CM-F the whole second table travels backwards while one Saberist retreats from a series of swings. Watch any of the Core Library from across a room and you can see which way the exchange is running.

CM-M is the movement that runs the other way, and it is worth being precise about what that means. The defending Saberist does not simply stand their ground. They step into the attack, take it at a shorter distance than it was thrown for, and end the beat closer to their partner than they began it. The attack was designed for one distance and it arrives at another, and that is the whole mechanism.

The notation shows it in the first four steps. Saberist B opens with a 7 and follows it with two completes, 2© and 5© — long, carried swings that need room. Saberist A does not take a single step back against any of them. The 7 is parried, the 2© is ducked, and the 5© is answered with a jump into a spin. Three attacks, three answers, and no ground given.

The cost of that is timing, and it falls on both Saberists. A completing swing thrown at a partner who is closing is a swing whose safe distance is changing while it travels, so Saberist B is committing to an arc that has to clear a target which is not where it was when the swing began. Saberist A has to be under the swing early, not on time. Late is not a smaller version of correct here; late is the blade arriving where the head is.

What the pressure buys is the turnover at step 5. Saberist A, having closed all the way through the opening, is already at the distance an attack needs — so the 4 and the 12 at steps 5 and 6 do not require a step forward to set them up. The defence has done that work. Saberist B recoils at step 7, spins away at step 8, and attacks on the 3 at step 9, and the exchange has changed hands twice in nine beats without either Saberist travelling to make it happen.

Then the movement stops dead. 3Pm6x against 9x binds the blades, and both rows carry x again at step 12, so the bind is held for two full beats. That is the only stillness in CM-M, and it sits directly after the busiest run in the movement. In performance it is where an audience catches up with what they have just watched.

Out of the bind come the two beats that make CM-M unmistakable. At step 13 both Saberists strike 1B, and at step 14 both strike 11B — the same bash, on the same line, on the same beat, from both sides. Nobody is defending. Two attacks meet in the middle twice in a row, and the identical cells in both rows are the notation saying exactly that. These are the two beats to set most carefully, because there is no parry in either row to control what happens if one Saberist is early.

The finish returns the movement to normal order: Saberist B attacks 12, Saberist A parries and recoils, and CM-M ends on a Special. After a sequence spent inverting the exchange, ending on an open slot is fitting — the last word belongs to the Saberists performing it.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-M is designed to teach:

  • answering an attack by closing distance rather than giving ground
  • turning a defence into forward pressure
  • reading a completing attack early enough to duck or jump it while advancing
  • spins as part of the exchange rather than decoration between beats
  • a parry written with a modifier, 3Pm6
  • holding a bind across beats with x
  • bashes struck by both Saberists on the same beat
  • passing the attack back and forth without either Saberist travelling to set it up

docs.title: Phase 1: Distance
docs.text:
Before any of the sequence is performed, agree the two distances the movement uses.

Stand at the distance Saberist B's completes are thrown for, then have Saberist A walk forward to the distance they will actually be answered at. Both Saberists should see how much shorter the second one is. Everything in CM-M depends on that gap being understood before it is performed at speed.

docs.title: Phase 2: The opening statically
docs.text:
Walk steps 1 to 4 one at a time, with a full stop after each.

Confirm at every step:

  • both Saberists agree which target the number names
  • the parry, duck or jump meets the attack cleanly
  • Saberist A finishes the step closer than they started it
  • the step can be repeated the same way

Perform the completes at half their eventual length for now.

docs.title: Phase 3: The duck and the jump-spin
docs.text:
Practise 2© against D, and 5© against J + S-CCW, as isolated pairs of beats.

These are the two most dangerous beats in the movement, because both are a carried swing answered by a Saberist who is moving toward it. Set the height of each swing and the timing of the answer slowly and by agreement, and repeat each pair until the two Saberists arrive together every time. The spin is added to the jump only once the jump alone is reliable.

docs.title: Phase 4: The turnover
docs.text:
Walk steps 5 to 10 one at a time.

This is where the attack changes hands, and the thing to watch is that neither Saberist steps to make it happen. If Saberist A has to move forward to reach the 4, the opening did not close enough distance — go back to Phase 2 rather than fixing it here.

docs.title: Phase 5: The bind and the bashes
docs.text:
Practise steps 11 and 12 as a held pair, then steps 13 and 14.

Enter the bind slowly and by agreement, and hold it for a full count of two before releasing. Then set the two bashes: they are struck simultaneously, so agree the line, the height and the meeting point for each, and run them at low speed for far longer than they appear to need.

docs.title: Phase 6: The finish
docs.text:
Decide what the Special will be, and run steps 15 to 17 as a unit.

Choose the special move before practice, not during it, and keep it the same every repetition. The recoil at step 16 is what sets it up, so the two are rehearsed together rather than separately.

docs.title: Phase 7: Slow continuous flow, then pace
docs.text:
Put all seventeen steps together at low speed, then bring the movement up to performance pace.

The seams are the entry to the bind, the exit from it, and the two bashes. Speed is added to the parries, the spins and the attacks; it is never added to the bind, the bashes or the jump.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-M should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

The hazard that belongs to this movement is the closing distance. Every other movement in the library is safe at a distance the pair sets once and keeps. CM-M is not: the distance shortens inside the opening by design, and it shortens while carried swings are in the air. The pair should set the closest point the movement reaches and rehearse there, rather than setting the starting distance and discovering the closest point at speed.

The two mutual bashes carry the same warning in a different form. Steps 13 and 14 have no parry in either row, which means neither Saberist is answering the other — both are attacking, and the blades meet because they were aimed to. Beats like that are agreed in advance, run slowly, and never accelerated to make them look stronger.

It is also worth naming what CM-M does to the notation. Nothing new was needed to write a sequence that runs backwards. The same target numbers, parries and completes describe an exchange moving toward the attacker instead of away from it, because the notation records what happens between two Saberists rather than which way the fight is drifting. Direction is something a movement has, not something the language has to be taught.

When CM-M is clean, continue to CM-N, which brings a second saber into the exchange, or return to the Extended Library.

docs.title: CM-N
docs.text:
CM-N is the library's introduction to dual wielding. Saberist A carries two sabers, Saberist B carries one, and the movement is written for that mismatch rather than around it.

It is deliberately short — six steps, the length of CM-A. The difficulty in dual wielding is not the sequence; it is the hands. Keeping the choreography brief leaves a Saberist free to spend their attention on which saber is working and when, which is the whole subject of the movement.

CM-N was notated by Cole Hemp.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
CM-N is written in a single table.

Wide tables

The table below is wide. On a phone, turn the device landscape; it can also be scrolled sideways.

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 Saberist A 11 3 7 CW - L>R 11 9 Saberist B 11P 3P 7P 11P 9P 1©

Read down each column as usual. Saberist A's row is the one that reads differently from every other movement in the library.

  • Saberist A holds two sabers. L stands for the left hand and R for the right, the same letters CM-K uses for the two ends of the staff. Which hand is working is part of the notation, not a detail left to the performer.
  • CW - L>R is the transfer, and it is the centre of the movement: a clockwise spin that moves the attack from the left hand to the right. It sits at step 4, dividing the sequence into three attacks before it and two after.
  • Saberist B holds one saber and answers everything. 11P, 3P, 7P, then 11P and 9P — five parries against five attacks, with nothing written on the beat where Saberist A transfers.
  • © is a complete, taught in CM-C. Saberist B's 1© at step 7 is the only attack in that row, it carries through rather than stopping, and nothing is written for Saberist A against it.
  • The target numbers are unchanged. An 11 is an 11 whichever hand throws it, and an 11P is the same parry it has always been. Two sabers add a question the notation has to answer — which hand — and change nothing else.
  • A blank cell means nothing is written for that Saberist on that beat. They hold while the other acts.

docs.title: Two sabers, one language
docs.text:
Everything before CM-N is written for Saberists holding one weapon each. Even CM-K, which brings in a staff, gives each Saberist a single thing to think about. CM-N is the first movement in which one Saberist has two, and the interesting part is how little the notation has to do about it.

It adds one piece of information: which hand. L and R are the same letters CM-K uses to say which end of the staff is coming, borrowed here to say which saber is coming, and that is the entire extra vocabulary. The lines are the lines. The parries are the parries. A movement written for four hands' worth of blade work reads exactly like a movement written for two.

What changes is what the Saberists have to do.

For Saberist A the difficulty is the off hand. Most people can strike an 11 cleanly with their dominant hand on the first afternoon and cannot do it at all with the other one. That is why CM-N is six steps long. A short sequence run many times gives the weaker hand the repetitions it needs, where a long sequence would simply let the Saberist hide the off hand behind the strong one and never fix it. If the off-hand strikes in this movement look worse than the strong-hand strikes, the movement is working — that gap is what it exists to close.

The transfer at step 4 is where those two halves meet. CW - L>R is a clockwise spin that hands the attack from the left saber to the right, and it is not decoration between beats. It is a beat in its own right, with nothing written for Saberist B against it, because a transfer takes time and the notation says so honestly rather than pretending the second saber arrives for free. Learn where both blades are throughout that spin before running it against a partner — one of them is travelling behind the Saberist's own line of sight.

For Saberist B the difficulty is that the attack can come from either side. Against a single saber, a defender learns the shape of an opponent's approach — where the blade lives, which shoulder the attacks fall from — and reads the next attack partly from habit. A dual wielder removes that. The 11 at step 1 and the 11 at step 5 are the same line and the same number, and they arrive from different hands. Saberist B has to parry the blade rather than the pattern, which is a harder thing and the reason the single-saber role in this movement is not the easy one.

The finish belongs to Saberist B, and it is deliberate. After five parries, a 1© carries through on the one beat the dual wielder has nothing written. The Saberist with fewer blades gets the last word, which is the movement's way of saying that two sabers are an advantage to be handled rather than an advantage in themselves.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-N is designed to teach:

  • carrying and striking with two sabers
  • L and R as the hand that strikes
  • building the off hand through a short sequence run many times
  • transferring the attack between hands with a spin, as a beat of its own
  • defending with a single saber against attacks that can arrive from either hand
  • reading the blade rather than the pattern
  • closing an exchange with a completing counter

docs.title: Phase 1: The second saber alone
docs.text:
Saberist A works both sabers with no partner and no sequence.

Hold one in each hand and strike the four lines the movement uses — 11, 3, 7 and 9 — first with the strong hand, then with the off hand, slowly and separately. Learn where the idle blade sits while the other one works. Everything else in CM-N depends on this, and it deserves a whole session before any of the sequence is attempted.

docs.title: Phase 2: The transfer
docs.text:
Practise CW - L>R on its own, without a partner.

The spin passes the attack from the left saber to the right, and both blades are moving while it happens. Take it at walking speed until the Saberist knows where each blade is at every point in the turn, and can arrive from it ready to strike rather than ready to recover.

docs.title: Phase 3: The opening attacks statically
docs.text:
Walk steps 1 to 3 one at a time, with a full stop after each.

Confirm at every step:

  • both Saberists agree which target the number names
  • Saberist A strikes with the hand the sequence calls for
  • the parry meets the attack cleanly, at a distance safe for both of Saberist A's blades
  • the step can be repeated the same way

docs.title: Phase 4: After the transfer
docs.text:
Add step 4, then walk steps 5 and 6 the same way.

Saberist B does nothing on the transfer beat. That is a real pause and it should be held rather than hurried through — Saberist B waits for the attack to come out of the spin instead of anticipating it.

docs.title: Phase 5: The counter
docs.text:
Practise Saberist B's 1© on its own.

It is a complete, so it carries through rather than stopping, and it lands on a beat where Saberist A has nothing written. Set its length and the distance it needs by agreement, and rehearse it as the end of the movement rather than as a seventh attack.

docs.title: Phase 6: Slow continuous flow, then pace
docs.text:
Run all seven beats without stopping at low speed, then add speed.

Speed goes to the parries and to the strong-hand attacks. It does not go to the transfer, and it does not go to the off-hand attacks until they are as clean slowly as the strong-hand ones. Repeat the whole movement often — it is short on purpose.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-N should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

Two hazards belong to this movement. The first is the blade nobody is watching. Saberist A has two, and while one is doing something the pair is looking at, the other is somewhere — beside a leg, behind a shoulder, coming round in a spin. The lesson CM-K teaches about the far end of a staff applies here with a second saber in place of it, and the distance is set for both blades rather than for the one being used.

The second is the off hand itself. A hand that cannot yet control a strike will throw one that lands short, long or on the wrong line, and CM-N puts exactly such strikes in front of a partner by design. That is safe only at low speed and at a distance chosen for a swing that misses its mark. Off-hand work stays slow for far longer than it feels it needs to.

It is also worth naming what dual wielding did to the notation, because the answer is almost nothing. A single letter in front of an attack was enough to carry a second saber through a whole movement — the same letter, doing the same job, that carried a staff through CM-K. The notation describes what happens between two Saberists rather than how many blades either of them is holding, and CM-N is the shortest proof of that in the library.

When CM-N is clean, continue to CM-O, or return to the Extended Library.

docs.title: CM-O
docs.text:
CM-O, known in the school as Space Samurai, interprets the duel between Musashi and Tanaka from Westworld, Season 2, Episode 5.

It is the first movement in the library that is not a single sequence. CM-O joins two separate choreographies end to end and performs them as one continuous movement, which makes it the longest piece of unbroken choreography an Extended Library Saberist has met so far.

The notation is by Amen Abdou. Both roles are demonstrated in the lesson video by Amen Abdou and Alexis Adames.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
CM-O is written in four tables, read in order. The first two are the opening sequence; the last two are the sequence joined onto it.

Wide tables

The tables below are wide. On a phone, turn the device landscape; any of them can also be scrolled sideways.

Part 1

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 Saberist A (Tanaka) 7© 1© 9© 5© 12 1B 0 Saberist B (Musashi) Dodge L Dodge R Dodge Back Spin R>L 12P 1B 0P L>R

Part 2

Player s1 s2 s3 Saberist A (Tanaka) 7B 1X SS Saberist B (Musashi) 7B 1X SS (Push L)

Part 3

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 Saberist A (Tanaka) 4P 8P 4P 8P 1 9©-B 4 Saberist B (Musashi) 4 8 4 8 1P 7©-B 4

Part 4

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 Saberist A (Tanaka) 0 7P 5X 12X Saberist B (Musashi) 0P-UP 7 5X-M 12X (Ig)

Read down each column as usual, and read the four tables as one movement rather than four.

  • Part 1 belongs to Saberist A. Four completes in a row — 7©, 1©, 9©, 5© — and not one of them is parried. © is a complete, taught in CM-C, and Saberist B answers all four by leaving the line: Dodge L, Dodge R, Dodge Back, then Spin R>L.
  • The roles swap at Part 3. Saberist B attacks 4, 8, 4, 8 while Saberist A parries all four, and then the attack changes hands again at step 5, where 1 meets 1P.
  • B is a bash and X is a lock, both taught in CM-E. Steps 6 of Part 1 and 1 to 2 of Part 2 run 1B, then 7B, then 1X — with both Saberists writing the same cell each time.
  • SS is the saber stand-off, the prolonged lock listed as S+S in the Notation Legend. It ends Part 2, with Saberist B pushing left out of it.
  • 0 is a thrust, as in CM-D. It closes Part 1, answered by 0P L>R, and opens Part 4, answered by 0P-UP — a thrust parry taken upward.
  • Ig is the inverted grip from CM-J, and it appears in the last cell of the movement: Saberist B locks 12X in an inverted grip against Saberist A's 12X.
  • Step 7 of Part 3 is written 4 in both rows, and step 6 pairs a complete on the 9 line against a complete on the 7 line. The demonstration video shows how both beats resolve.
  • Both locks in Part 4 are held. 5X against 5X-M and 12X against 12X (Ig) finish the movement bound rather than struck.

docs.title: Telegraph
docs.text:
Saberist A steps forward, bends the front knee at 45°, places the saber at the rear hip as if holstered, and tilts the head forward as if to lunge.

The telegraph is the silent signal that calls CM-O before an exchange begins. See LUMINA Games for how telegraphs are used in play.

docs.title: Two sequences in one movement
docs.text:
Every movement so far has been one sequence. It has a telegraph, a shape, a finish, and when the finish arrives the movement is over. CM-O is two of those, performed without stopping between them, and that changes what a Saberist has to hold in their head.

The joining place is what makes it work. Part 1 ends on a thrust and its parry; Part 2 opens with a mutual bash and closes in a stand-off; Part 3 opens with the attack in the other Saberist's hands. Nothing announces the seam. There is no reset, no return to guard, no second telegraph — the stand-off simply releases and the second sequence is already running.

That is why the stand-off is where it is. SS is a prolonged lock, held while both Saberists are bound and neither is moving, and it is the one point in a long movement where the pair can find each other again. It absorbs the seam: whatever was slightly early or slightly late in Part 1 is corrected inside the hold, and both Saberists come out of it together into Part 3. A join placed anywhere else would need the pair to be in perfect agreement at speed. Placed at a lock, it needs only that they arrive.

The two halves are also built differently, and running them back to back is the point of the exercise.

Part 1 is asymmetric. One Saberist attacks with four carried completes and the other never touches them, answering with Dodge L, Dodge R, Dodge Back and a spin. That is CM-F's lesson — the body leaving the line instead of the blade meeting it — but performed with a saber in hand, against completes, and while the dodges themselves travel left, right and backwards. A Saberist who dodges late here has nothing to fall back on, because a complete does not stop.

Part 3 is symmetric. 4, 8, 4, 8 against 4P, 8P, 4P, 8P is the plainest attack-and-parry writing in the Extended Library — four beats where both rows say the same thing about the same lines, and the only difference is the P. After the dodges of Part 1 it reads as the fight settling into a rhythm, which is exactly what a repeated four-beat exchange does to an audience.

Then the movement ends on locks rather than a strike. 5X and 12X bind twice in the last three beats, the second with Saberist B in an inverted grip, and CM-O finishes with both blades held together and neither Saberist struck. A movement that opened with four unanswered swings ends with nothing moving at all.

The demand this makes is stamina of attention rather than of body. Eleven steps into a twenty-one step movement, both Saberists are still inside choreography they agreed on a minute earlier, with no reset to recover from a mistake. Lose the count in Part 3 and there is no telegraph to catch it. That is the skill CM-O trains, and it is the reason to keep the two halves as one piece rather than teaching them as two.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-O is designed to teach:

  • performing two sequences as one continuous movement with no reset between them
  • holding a long count without a telegraph to recover on
  • dodging completing attacks with a saber still in hand
  • using a stand-off as the seam that joins two sequences
  • symmetric attack-and-parry rhythm across repeated lines
  • thrusts and their parries, taken both across and upward
  • finishing a movement on a lock rather than a strike
  • locking in an inverted grip

docs.title: Phase 1: Part 1 statically
docs.text:
Walk the seven steps of Part 1 one at a time, with a full stop after each.

Confirm at every step:

  • both Saberists agree which target the number names
  • the dodge leaves the line the complete is travelling on
  • the complete is thrown at a length both Saberists have agreed
  • the step can be repeated the same way

The four completes are the reason to take this slowly. A dodge cannot be late, because there is no blade in the way of a swing that carries through.

docs.title: Phase 2: Part 3 statically
docs.text:
Walk the seven steps of Part 3 the same way.

The four repeated beats — 4, 8, 4, 8 — are the easiest material in the movement and the easiest to run mechanically. Take them as four separate attacks with four separate parries, and only let them become a rhythm once each one is correct on its own.

docs.title: Phase 3: The bashes, the lock and the stand-off
docs.text:
Practise Part 2 as three isolated beats.

Both Saberists write 7B and then 1X on the same beats, so both are moving toward the other with nothing defending. Set the meeting point for the bash, enter the lock slowly and by agreement, and then hold the stand-off for a full count before Saberist B pushes left out of it. This is the join between the two halves, and it deserves its own session.

docs.title: Phase 4: The finish
docs.text:
Practise Part 4 on its own.

The thrust and its upward parry come first, then two locks in three beats, the last one taken in an inverted grip. Set the grip change before the lock rather than during it, and enter both locks slowly, as always.

docs.title: Phase 5: Each half continuously
docs.text:
Run Part 1 into Part 2, and Part 3 into Part 4, as two separate runs.

Each half should be reliable end to end at low speed before the two are joined. If either Saberist loses the sequence, restart that half from its first step rather than picking it up mid-phrase.

docs.title: Phase 6: The whole movement
docs.text:
Join the halves at the stand-off and run all twenty-one steps without stopping.

Expect the count to be the difficulty rather than any single beat. Run it slowly and completely, many times, before any of it is brought up to speed.

docs.title: Phase 7: Performance pace
docs.text:
Add speed to the dodges and to the four repeated beats of Part 3, and leave the bashes, the locks and the stand-off where they are.

CM-O should read as one movement that changes character halfway through, not as two movements played in sequence. Holding the stand-off at its rehearsed length is what makes the join disappear.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-O should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

Two hazards belong to this movement. The first is the opening: four completes in a row, none of them parried, answered only by a Saberist moving out of the way. Nothing stops those swings if a dodge is late, so the length of each complete is agreed before it is ever thrown at speed, and the dodges are rehearsed at full commitment from the first repetition. The second is the pair of mutual bashes, where both rows carry the same cell and neither Saberist is defending — beats like that are set slowly and never accelerated.

Length is a hazard in its own right here. Twenty-one steps with no reset is long enough for concentration to drift, and a movement is at its least safe on the beat after attention has wandered. Run CM-O in halves for longer than seems necessary, and stop the moment either Saberist starts to search for the next step.

It is also worth telling students what joining two sequences means for the notation. Nothing was added to the language to do it. Four tables in order are read exactly as one table in order would be, because the notation numbers steps within a sequence and says nothing about how many sequences a performance contains. That is what makes longer choreography possible without a longer vocabulary.

When CM-O is clean, continue to CM-P, or return to the Extended Library.

docs.title: CM-P
docs.text:
CM-P interprets the duel between Count Dooku and Anakin Skywalker in Star Wars: Episode III — Revenge of the Sith, the same fight CM-M draws on.

At twenty-eight steps it is the longest movement in the Extended Library, and it is the first one written all the way to a conclusion. The exchanges do not simply stop when the sequence runs out: one Saberist goes to the ground, loses the saber, and the other picks it up. CM-P is choreography for the end of a fight.

CM-P was notated by Kristianna Jones, assisted by Victoria de Cun.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
CM-P runs twenty-eight steps, written in three tables read in order.

Wide tables

The tables below are wide. On a phone, turn the device landscape; any of them can also be scrolled sideways.

Part 1

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 s9 s10 Saberist A Kick 4 9 5 7B 5© Plum 1x 180 P CC 1B Saberist B Drama 4P 9P Inv 5P 7B Jump back Plum Turn CC 1PX 180 Spin away 1B

Part 2

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 s9 s10 Saberist A 7B 1B 12 5B 7B 3 3P Inv 1 12 3X Saberist B 7B 1B 12P 5B 7B 3P Inv 3 1P 12P 3P X

Part 3

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 Saberist A 12 R 11@ Turn CW 9 BB 12 Px Step side 12 push Take saber Saberist B 11 @ 12R Turn CCW 9 P Inv 12 X Fall 0 Saber down

Read down each column as usual. The thing to watch across all three tables is how often both rows carry the same cell.

  • B is a bash, from CM-E, and CM-P is built on it. 7B in Part 1, then 7B, 1B, 5B, 7B through Part 2 — and in every one of those beats both Saberists write the same cell, so both are striking rather than one answering the other.
  • Plum is the plum flourish, listed as Fl-OA in the Notation Legend. Both Saberists perform it at step 7 of Part 1, Saberist B turning counter clockwise out of it.
  • © is a complete, taught in CM-C. Saberist A's 5© at step 6 of Part 1 carries through, which is why Saberist B answers it with Jump back rather than a parry.
  • X is a lock and x holds into the next move. 1x 180 against 1PX 180 binds the blades and turns the pair 180° while they are bound; Part 2 closes on 3X against 3P X; Part 3 locks again at 12 Px against 12 X.
  • The attack changes hands repeatedly in Part 2. Steps 6 and 7 trade it inside two beats: 3 against 3P Inv, then 3P Inv against 3, the same pair of cells swapped between the rows.
  • Inv marks several parries — 9P Inv, 3P Inv, 9 P Inv — and Kick is the opening beat, listed as K in the Notation Legend.
  • Part 3 opens on a swap. Saberist A's 12 R meets Saberist B's 11 @, and on the next beat the two cells change places. Both Saberists then turn, one clockwise and one counter clockwise.
  • The movement ends with a fall and a disarm. Saberist B's last cells are Fall 0 and Saber down; Saberist A's are 12 push and Take saber. Nothing is written for Saberist B on the final beat.
  • Some cells are written in the lesson's own shorthand — Drama, P CC, 9 BB, 11@. The demonstration video shows those beats.

docs.title: Telegraph
docs.text:
Claw, then position 1.

The telegraph is the silent signal that calls CM-P before an exchange begins. See LUMINA Games for how telegraphs are used in play.

docs.title: Bashing, and a fight that ends
docs.text:
Most movements are an argument between an attack and an answer. One row says 1, the other says 1P, and the exchange is a conversation in which each Saberist is doing something different from the other. CM-P spends a great deal of its length doing away with that.

Look at Part 2. Steps 1, 2, 4 and 5 are 7B, 1B, 5B, 7B — and both rows are identical on every one. Neither Saberist is defending. Two blades are driven at the same line at the same moment and stopped against each other, four times in five beats. That is a bash used the way this movement uses it: not as a way to break a guard, but as the sound of two people who have stopped trying to out-fence one another.

It has a specific effect in performance, and it is worth naming for students. A parry reads as skill — someone saw the attack and answered it. A mutual bash reads as force, because nobody answered anything. A run of them reads as a fight that has become a struggle. That is the shape the middle of CM-P is drawing, and it is why the bashes come in runs rather than singly.

It is also why they are the most carefully rehearsed beats on the page. In every other movement, a mistimed attack meets a parry that was placed to receive it. Here there is no parry in either row, so the only thing keeping a mutual bash safe is that both Saberists agreed on the line, the height and the meeting point beforehand and have not drifted from it.

Between the runs, the movement keeps handing the attack back and forth faster than anything before it. Steps 6 and 7 of Part 2 are the clearest case: 3 against 3P Inv, and then exactly the same two cells with the rows exchanged. The attack is taken, answered, and returned in two beats. Part 3 opens the same way, with 12 R and 11 @ swapping places between steps 1 and 2. A Saberist who thinks of themselves as the attacker or the defender for any length of time will be behind in this movement, because the roles change every second or third beat.

Then there is the finish, and it is what makes CM-P different from everything before it.

Every movement so far ends because the notation runs out. The last attack is parried, or the blades bind, or a special move closes the phrase, and the two Saberists are still standing in the same relationship they started in. CM-P ends because one of them loses. Saberist B thrusts and falls, the saber goes down, Saberist A pushes on the 12 line and picks the weapon up. Eight beats of Part 3 do what the previous twenty could not: they settle the fight.

That asks something new of both Saberists. Saberist B has to fall — deliberately, on a chosen line, in a controlled way, while holding a saber they are about to give up. Saberist A has to take a weapon from a partner who is on the ground, which means arriving at a known place at a known speed, with a hand-off both have practised. Neither is a fencing skill. Both are performance skills, and CM-P is where the library asks for them.

The reason to learn a movement written to a conclusion is that a duel in performance needs one. A sequence that stops is a drill; a sequence that resolves is a scene. Everything CM-P teaches before Part 3 — the bash runs, the fast handovers, the bound turn — is arranged so that the fall, when it comes, reads as the outcome of what happened rather than as the point at which the choreography ran out.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-P is designed to teach:

  • sustaining a twenty-eight step movement across three tables
  • bashes struck by both Saberists on the same line and the same beat
  • runs of bashes as the shape of a fight rather than as single events
  • passing the attack back and forth every few beats
  • turning 180° with the blades bound
  • the plum flourish performed by both Saberists together
  • staging a controlled fall as part of choreography
  • finishing a movement with a disarm taken from the ground

docs.title: Phase 1: Part 1 statically
docs.text:
Walk the ten steps of Part 1 one at a time, with a full stop after each.

Confirm at every step:

  • both Saberists agree which target the number names
  • the parry, jump or bash meets the attack cleanly
  • the opening kick is thrown to an agreed target, at an agreed distance, with no contact
  • the step can be repeated the same way

Perform the complete at step 6 at half its eventual length for now.

docs.title: Phase 2: The flourish and the bound turn
docs.text:
Practise step 7 and step 8 of Part 1 as isolated beats.

Both Saberists flourish at the same moment, so agree the timing before either moves. Then set the bound turn: the blades meet on the 1 line, hold, and the pair rotates 180° together. Enter it slowly, every time, and agree which way the turn goes before it is attempted.

docs.title: Phase 3: The bash runs
docs.text:
Practise the four bashes of Part 2 as a block, at low speed.

This is the most important phase in the movement and the one to spend the most time on. For each of 7B, 1B, 5B and 7B, both Saberists set the line, the height and the exact point where the blades meet, and then repeat it until it is identical every time. Nothing in either row defends, so the agreement is the safety.

docs.title: Phase 4: The handovers
docs.text:
Walk steps 6 to 10 of Part 2 one at a time.

The attack changes hands twice inside these five beats. Take them slowly enough that both Saberists can say out loud, at each step, which of them is attacking — and keep taking them slowly until neither has to.

docs.title: Phase 5: Part 3 to the fall
docs.text:
Walk steps 1 to 5 of Part 3, ending at the lock.

The two opening cells swap between the rows, and the turns go opposite ways, so this is a short block that is easy to mirror incorrectly. Confirm the direction of each turn before running it.

docs.title: Phase 6: The fall and the disarm
docs.text:
Practise the last three steps on their own, on a floor that has been checked.

Saberist B sets the fall first, without a saber in hand, until it is safe and repeatable. Then it is rehearsed holding the saber, then with the saber going down on an agreed spot. Only then is the hand-off added: Saberist A steps in and takes the saber from a known place, at walking speed. This block is never brought up to performance pace.

docs.title: Phase 7: Continuous flow, then pace
docs.text:
Run each part end to end, then all twenty-eight steps at low speed, and only then add speed.

Speed belongs to the attacks, parries and handovers. It does not belong to the bashes, the bound turn, the fall or the disarm, and CM-P reads better when the ending is slower than the middle.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-P should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

Three hazards belong to this movement, and all three are unusual. The first is the volume of mutual bashes: six beats across the movement where both rows carry the same cell and neither Saberist is defending. The second is the bound 180° turn, where the pair rotates with the blades together and each Saberist loses sight of the other partway through. The third is the fall, which is the only time in the library a Saberist goes to the ground inside a sequence — it is rehearsed on a checked floor, on its own, without a weapon before with one, and it is never accelerated.

The disarm at the end deserves its own note. A saber is taken from a partner who is lying down, which means the two Saberists are at very different heights and one of them cannot move away. Agree exactly where the saber lands, exactly where Saberist A stands to collect it, and treat the whole beat as a hand-off rather than as a grab.

It is also worth naming what a written ending does for a performance. The notation did not need a new symbol to say that a fight is over — a fall, a saber down and a saber taken are written in the same cells as any other action. What the sequence gains is a shape: a beginning that opens with a kick, a middle that grinds through bashes, and an end that resolves. That is a scene rather than an exchange, and it is what the Extended Library has been building toward.

When CM-P is clean, continue to CM-Q, or return to the Extended Library.

docs.title: CM-R
docs.text:
CM-R interprets Ronin's battle against the Yakuza boss in Avengers: Endgame.

It is the least blade-driven movement in the Extended Library. Attacks and parries are there, but the beats that decide the exchange are pulls, shoves, a retreat, a pose and a fall — actions written into the notation exactly as a 3P or a 12 would be. CM-R is where a Saberist learns that everything a scene needs can be written down, not only the swordplay.

CM-R was notated by Luis Meurice.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
CM-R is written in two tables, read in order.

Wide tables

Both tables below are wide. On a phone, turn the device landscape; either table can also be scrolled sideways.

Part 1

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 s9 s10 Saberist A Blend 90 L Lh Ig 11 Lh Ig P3 S+ (Pull right) Step Back Duck + Special Flourish 3P S+ Pull right Saberist B 12 3X Pull left Shove 10© Retreat + Pose 3X Pull left Down hard

Part 2

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 s9 Saberist A Special Pose Step back 12P 9P Special + push back Blend 180 L Blend 180 L 12 Saberist B retreat 6© 12B 9B 0 1© 0

Read down each column as usual. Count how many cells name something other than a target line — that is what this movement is about.

  • Lh is left handed and Ig is the inverted grip, both in the Notation Legend, and CM-R opens with them stacked: Lh Ig 11 is an 11 struck left-handed in an inverted grip, and Lh Ig P3 is the matching parry. The grip is the one taught in CM-J.
  • X is a lock, from CM-E, and S+ is the saber stand-off — the prolonged lock listed as S+S in the Notation Legend. Both stand-offs in this movement are written with what each Saberist does to break them: Pull right against Pull left.
  • Blends are written as turns here. CM-F writes a blend with the line it works on, Blend 1 Left. CM-R writes it with the angle the body travels through instead — Blend 90 L in Part 1, and Blend 180 L twice in Part 2, each one turning away from a thrust or a complete.
  • © is a complete, taught in CM-C; B is a bash and 0 is a thrust, as in CM-D. Saberist B's row carries all of them: 10©, 6©, 12B, 9B, 0, 1©, 0.
  • Special appears three times, in the sense CM-E gives it — the notation names the slot, and the Saberists performing it choose what fills it. Two of the three are attached to something else: Duck + Special and Special + push back.
  • Shove, Pose, Retreat + Pose, Flourish, Step Back and Down hard are beats in their own right. They occupy a step each, and the other Saberist is answering them.
  • A blank cell means nothing is written for that Saberist on that beat. They hold while the other acts.

docs.title: Pulls, shoves and poses
docs.text:
A lock is a problem the notation has never had to solve. Two blades bind, both Saberists hold, and then — in every movement up to now — the sequence simply continues, because the next cell says what each Saberist does next and the bind is over by implication.
