CM-R stops taking that for granted. Both of its stand-offs are written with an instruction for getting out: S+ (Pull right) against Pull left, twice.

That pairing is worth reading carefully, because it is not a fight over the blades. The two Saberists pull in opposite directions, which means neither is trying to overpower the other and both are moving to a place they agreed on beforehand. A stand-off broken by force is a wrestling match with two lit blades in it. A stand-off broken by two people pulling apart on an agreed count looks, from the outside, exactly like the first thing and is nothing like it. Learning to write and rehearse the exit is the point.

The same principle runs through the rest of the movement. Shove at step 5 of Part 1 is Saberist B putting hands on Saberist A, and it works because Saberist A's cell says Step Back — the shove does not move anybody; the person being shoved moves. Special + push back in Part 2 is the same trade in the other direction. Down hard is Saberist B going to the ground on the last beat of Part 1, with nothing written for Saberist A, because a fall belongs entirely to the Saberist doing it.

Then there are the beats that are pure performance. Retreat + Pose at step 7 of Part 1, answered by Flourish. Pose again at step 2 of Part 2. These are two Saberists standing apart, doing nothing to each other, and the notation gives them a full step each. That is a deliberate choice by the notator and a good one: a filmed fight is mostly not contact, and a movement that only writes down the contact will always play faster and flatter than the scene it came from. The pose is where an audience is told what just happened mattered.

The blade work that remains is arranged around all of this rather than the other way round. Saberist A opens left-handed in an inverted grip — the least familiar way to hold a saber, chosen for the first two beats of the movement — and the exchange proper does not arrive until Part 2, where 12B and 9B meet 12P and 9P and two thrusts are answered by 180° blends. Even there, the blends are written as turns rather than lines, so what the notation is describing is a body moving through an angle, with the blade following it.

The last three beats show what the movement has been building. Blend 180 L twice, against a complete and then a thrust, and then Saberist A attacks 12 with nothing written in answer. After a movement spent pulling, shoving, retreating and posing, it ends on a plain attack that nobody replies to — and it lands as a conclusion precisely because everything before it was not.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-R is designed to teach:

  • striking and parrying left-handed in an inverted grip
  • blends written as a turn through an angle rather than along a line
  • breaking a stand-off by pulling apart on an agreed count
  • shoves, pushes and retreats as written, rehearsed beats
  • staging a controlled fall
  • poses and flourishes as steps that carry a scene
  • placing Special slots inside a movement rather than only at its end

docs.title: Phase 1: The inverted grip, left-handed
docs.text:
Saberist A works Lh Ig 11 and Lh Ig P3 with no partner.

This is the least natural position in the movement and it is the first thing in it. Strike the 11 line and take the 3 parry, left-handed, in the inverted grip, slowly and repeatedly, until both are controlled. Nothing else in CM-R should be attempted until they are.

docs.title: Phase 2: The stand-offs and the pulls
docs.text:
Practise S+ with Pull right against Pull left, as an isolated pair of beats.

Enter the bind slowly, hold it, and then break it by pulling in opposite directions on an agreed count. Neither Saberist is trying to win the bind. Set the direction, the count and the distance each one travels, and rehearse it until the exit happens the same way every time — both stand-offs in the movement use it.

docs.title: Phase 3: The shove, the push and the fall
docs.text:
Practise Shove against Step Back, Special + push back, and Down hard, one at a time.

For the shoves, agree exactly where the hands go and remember that the Saberist being shoved provides the movement. For the fall, work on a floor that has been checked, without a saber first, then holding one. This block is never brought up to performance speed.

docs.title: Phase 4: Part 1 statically
docs.text:
Walk the ten steps of Part 1 one at a time, with a full stop after each.

Confirm at every step:

  • both Saberists agree which target the number names
  • the parry, blend or duck meets the attack cleanly
  • the pulls, shoves and the fall happen exactly as rehearsed in Phases 2 and 3
  • the step can be repeated the same way

docs.title: Phase 5: Part 2 statically
docs.text:
Walk the nine steps of Part 2 the same way.

This is where most of the blade work lives — two bashes, two thrusts, a complete — and it is also where both 180° blends are. Take the blends as turns: the body leaves first and the blade follows, and the Saberist should finish each one facing where the sequence needs them to be.

docs.title: Phase 6: The specials and the poses
docs.text:
Decide what each Special will be, and rehearse the poses at their full length.

Choose all three specials before practice, not during it, and keep them the same every repetition. Then hold Retreat + Pose and Pose for the count they will actually be performed at — the temptation is to rush them, and rushing them removes the reason they are written.

docs.title: Phase 7: Continuous flow, then pace
docs.text:
Run each part end to end at low speed, then join them and add speed.

Speed belongs to the attacks, parries and blends. It does not belong to the stand-offs, the pulls, the shove, the fall or the poses, and CM-R reads better when the quiet beats are given more time rather than less.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-R should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

The hazards in this movement are almost all hand-to-hand rather than blade-to-blade, which makes them easy to underestimate. Two Saberists pull against each other twice, one shoves the other, one pushes back, and one goes to the ground hard — all while both are holding lit blades. Every one of those beats is rehearsed on its own, at walking speed, with the contact points agreed out loud, before it is ever run inside the sequence. A pair that would never speed up a lock will happily speed up a shove, and the shove is the one that puts a hand where a blade is about to be.

The opening carries its own warning. Left-handed work in an inverted grip is the least controlled way most Saberists can hold a saber, and CM-R asks for it in the first two beats, cold. It belongs in a warm-up long before it belongs in a run-through.

It is also worth naming what this movement does for the notation. A shove, a retreat, a pose and a fall are written in the same cells, on the same beats, as an 11 or a 3P. Nothing needed to be added to the language to record them, because the notation writes down what happens between two Saberists rather than what their blades do. CM-R is the clearest evidence in the library that choreography and swordplay are not the same subject.

When CM-R is clean, continue to CM-S, which builds a movement out of a shape, or return to the Extended Library.

docs.title: CM-S
docs.text:
CM-S shows that a movement can be built out of anything — including a shape. It takes the design of the letter S, runs it, then flips it and runs it the other way, and it introduces the lock spin: two Saberists bind their blades and turn their bodies together through the stand-off.

Nothing in the library before this one was drawn before it was notated. CM-S was, and that is the reason it is worth learning even before the lock spin is.

CM-S was notated by Spencer Jock.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
CM-S is written in two tables, read in order.

Wide tables

Both tables below are wide. On a phone, turn the device landscape; either table can also be scrolled sideways.

Part 1

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 s9 s10 Saberist A 1 10©A 3 5©A 7X SS+ SX-CCW 11 2©A 9 Saberist B 1P Duck 3P Jump 7X SS+ SX-CCW 11P Duck 9P

Part 2

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 s9 Saberist A 7©A 5X SS+ SX-CW Pause 12 12 3P Special Saberist B Jump 5PX SS+ SX-CW Pause B1-L B1-R S3

Read down each column as usual. The two tables are the same shape twice, turned the opposite way the second time.

  • ©A is a complete across — a complete carried wide, vertically across — listed in the Notation Legend. CM-S is full of them: 10©A, 5©A, 2©A, 7©A, and every one is answered by leaving the line rather than meeting it, with a Duck or a Jump.
  • X is a lock, from CM-E, and SS+ is the saber stand-off, the prolonged lock listed as S+S in the Notation Legend. Each half of the movement locks, holds the stand-off, and then spins out of it.
  • SX-CCW and SX-CW are the lock spins. They are written in both rows at the same step, because a lock spin is one action performed by two people: the blades stay bound and both Saberists turn, counter clockwise in Part 1 and clockwise in Part 2.
  • Pause is a written beat. It follows the second lock spin, and it is held rather than passed through.
  • Part 2 answers Part 1. Both halves open with a complete across, close into a lock, hold a stand-off and spin — the second one turning the other way. That reversal is the shape the movement is named for.
  • Special closes the movement, in the sense CM-E gives it: the notation names the slot, and the Saberists performing it choose what fills it.
  • B1-L, B1-R and S3 are written in the lesson's own shorthand. They are Saberist B's three beats after the pause — the first two answering Saberist A's repeated 12, the third answered by Saberist A's 3P. The demonstration video shows them.

docs.title: Telegraph
docs.text:
Draw a line in front of you across the ground.

The telegraph is the silent signal that calls CM-S before an exchange begins. See LUMINA Games for how telegraphs are used in play.

docs.title: The lock spin
docs.text:
A lock stops a fight. Two blades bind, both Saberists hold, and for as long as the bind lasts nothing travels — which is why locks are used as rests, as in CM-L, and as finishes, as in CM-O. A lock spin takes that still moment and makes it move.

The action is simple to describe and hard to do. The blades stay bound; both Saberists turn their bodies around the point where the blades meet; the bind is still there when they come out the other side. Notice how the notation writes it: SX-CCW appears in both rows, at the same step, spelled identically. That is unusual and it is deliberate. A 1 against a 1P is two Saberists doing different things that fit together. A lock spin is two Saberists doing the same thing, and the cell says so.

That single detail is the whole safety lesson. In an ordinary lock, each Saberist can hold their own blade steady and the bind stays where it is. In a lock spin, both are moving, so the bind only survives if both are moving at the same rate around the same centre. If one turns faster, the blades slide; if one turns wider, the bind opens. Neither Saberist can fix this alone, and neither can rescue it once it starts to go — which is why the stand-off comes first. SS+ sits immediately before both spins, and its job is to give the pair a held, settled bind to begin turning from.

The rest of CM-S exists to put the spin somewhere it makes sense, and this is where the shape comes in. Each half of the movement runs a line of attacks, gathers into a lock, holds, and turns — and then the second half does the same thing with the turn reversed. SX-CCW in Part 1, SX-CW in Part 2. Drawn on the floor by two Saberists moving, that is a curve, a turn, and a countercurve: the letter, and then the letter flipped. The telegraph tells you as much before the movement even starts, since it asks the Saberist to draw a line across the ground.

The attacks around the spins are chosen to keep that shape legible. Almost every one is a complete across, and every complete across is answered by a Duck or a Jump rather than a parry. That matters for the drawing: a parry stops an attack, and a stopped attack does not travel anywhere. A complete carried across, with the other Saberist dropping under it or leaving the ground over it, keeps the blade moving through its whole arc. The shape stays visible because nothing interrupts it.

Then there is the Pause. It comes directly after the second spin, and it is the only beat in the movement where the notation asks for nothing at all. Coming out of a lock spin, both Saberists are turned around, off their starting marks, and probably not quite where they expected to be. A written pause is how a notator says: arrive, settle, and let the audience see where you have ended up. Movements that leave that beat out play their best moment and then rush past it.

The finish is quick by comparison — two 12 attacks answered in succession, one exchange on the 3 line, and a Special — and it works because the shape has already been drawn. By that point CM-S has made its argument: a movement does not have to begin with a fight. It can begin with a line on the ground.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-S is designed to teach:

  • building a movement out of a shape rather than out of an exchange
  • the lock spin, and reading a cell that both Saberists perform identically
  • entering a spin from a settled stand-off rather than from a fresh bind
  • turning both directions, so the shape is drawn and then mirrored
  • completes across, answered by ducking and jumping rather than parrying
  • holding a written Pause after the movement's biggest action
  • closing with a Special

docs.title: Phase 1: Completes across, and the answers
docs.text:
Practise ©A on its own, with the ducks and jumps that answer it.

A complete across travels further than anything most Saberists have performed to this point, and four of them are in this movement. Set the height and the arc of each one, agree whether it is being ducked or jumped, and rehearse each pair until the two Saberists arrive together. Nothing carrying that much blade is run at speed early.

docs.title: Phase 2: The stand-off
docs.text:
Practise the lock into SS+, held, without the spin.

Enter the bind slowly, settle it, and hold it for a full count. Both Saberists should be able to feel where the blades meet without looking at them. That contact point is the centre the spin will turn around, and it has to be reliable before anything rotates.

docs.title: Phase 3: The lock spin, one direction
docs.text:
Add SX-CCW to the stand-off, at walking pace.

Turn together, slowly, one step at a time, keeping the bind. If the blades slide, stop and restart from the stand-off rather than correcting mid-turn. Both Saberists are performing the same action, so both should be counting it the same way — out loud, at first.

docs.title: Phase 4: The lock spin, the other direction
docs.text:
Practise SX-CW the same way, then the Pause that follows it.

Reversing the turn is not automatic. The footwork changes, the bind is approached from the other side, and a pair comfortable with one direction will often be clumsy in the other. Give it its own session, and finish each repetition by holding the pause at full length.

docs.title: Phase 5: Part 1 statically
docs.text:
Walk the ten steps of Part 1 one at a time, with a full stop after each.

Confirm at every step:

  • both Saberists agree which target the number names
  • the duck or jump leaves the line the complete across is travelling on
  • the lock, stand-off and spin happen exactly as rehearsed
  • the step can be repeated the same way

docs.title: Phase 6: Part 2 statically
docs.text:
Walk the nine steps of Part 2 the same way, and decide what the Special will be.

Choose the special move before practice rather than during it, and keep it the same every repetition.

docs.title: Phase 7: Continuous flow, then pace
docs.text:
Run each half end to end at low speed, join them, and only then add speed.

Speed belongs to the attacks and the answers. It does not belong to the stand-offs, the spins or the pause. CM-S should read as a shape being drawn steadily, and a rushed lock spin is both the least safe and the least legible thing in it.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-S should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

The lock spin is the hazard, and it is a hazard of a kind the library has not presented before. Every other dangerous beat in the Extended Library is dangerous because one Saberist might be early or late. A lock spin is dangerous because two Saberists are turning while bound, so a mistake is not one blade arriving wrongly — it is a bind coming apart between two people who are both already committed to a rotation. Enter it only from a settled stand-off, turn at walking pace for far longer than seems necessary, and stop the whole movement rather than trying to save a spin that has started to slide.

The completes across carry the ordinary warning in a larger form. They are long, they are carried, and they are answered by a partner who is ducking under or jumping over them, so the height of each one is agreed and fixed before speed is added anywhere.

It is also worth telling students what CM-S is doing in the library at all. It is not an interpretation of a filmed fight and it does not come out of an exchange between two people. It began as a letter, and the choreography was fitted to it. That is a legitimate way to make a movement, and the notation records it no differently from anything else — which means a Saberist with a shape, a story or an idea has everything they need to write it down.

When CM-S is clean, continue to CM-T, or return to the Extended Library.

docs.title: CM-T
docs.text:
CM-T is about flow spins and holds — the two things that happen between attacks.

Spins carry the movement from one exchange to the next, in both directions and sometimes in opposite directions at the same moment. Holds stop it: a lock carried into the next beat, a pause written into a step, and a one-handed hold at the very end. Twenty-two steps of choreography, and a good deal of it is neither an attack nor a parry.

CM-T was notated by Thom Timko and Mario Cubas.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
CM-T runs twenty-two steps, written in three tables read in order.

Wide tables

The tables below are wide. On a phone, turn the device landscape; any of them can also be scrolled sideways.

Part 1

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 s9 s10 Saberist A 3P 9P 3P 9P 3P (behind) S CW 9P IgX x 12 X Saberist B 6P 3 9 3 9X S CW 3X S CCW 9X x 12P X

Part 2

Player s11 s12 s13 s14 s15 s16 s17 s18 s19 s20 Saberist A St-F St-B (pause) Fl-Overhead 4B S CCW 1 8 4 10 D S CCW Saberist B St-F St-B (pause) Fl-Overhead 4B S CCW 1P 8P 4P 10P 2©

Part 3

Player s21 s22 Saberist A Bl-3 1H (hold at bay) Saberist B 12©

Read down each column as usual, and watch for the steps where both rows say the same thing.

  • S CW and S CCW are spins, clockwise and counter clockwise, listed in the Notation Legend. There are five, and they are the movement's connective tissue rather than its decoration. At step 8 both Saberists spin at once, in opposite directions.
  • X is a lock and x carries a lock into the next move, both from CM-E. Step 10 uses them together in both rows — x 12 X against x 12P X — so a bind is held out of step 9 and closed into a new one on the 12 line.
  • Ig is the inverted grip from CM-J. 9P IgX at step 9 is a 9 parry taken in the inverted grip and bound into a lock, against Saberist B's 9X.
  • 3P (behind) is a parry taken behind the back, at step 7, against a lock on the same line.
  • Steps 11 to 15 are written identically in both rows. St-F, St-B (pause), Fl-Overhead, 4B, S CCW — step forward, step back and hold, an overhead flourish, a bash, and a spin, all performed by both Saberists together. St-F and St-B are footwork and Fl-Overhead is the overhead flourish, listed as Fl-H in the Notation Legend.
  • B is a bash; © is a complete, taught in CM-C; Bl- is a blend, as in CM-F; D is a duck and 1H is one handed, both in the Notation Legend. The movement ends on 1H (hold at bay) against a 12©.
  • A blank cell means nothing is written for that Saberist on that beat. They hold while the other acts.

docs.title: Flow spins and holds
docs.text:
Take the attacks out of CM-T and there is still a movement left. That is not true of anything earlier in the library, and it is the reason this one exists.

Start with the spins. There are five, and none of them is an attack, a parry or an evasion. Step 6 is a spin alone for Saberist B, on a beat where Saberist A has nothing written. Step 8 is a spin for both Saberists, and they go opposite ways — S CW against S CCW. Step 15 is a spin performed by both in the same direction. Step 20 combines a spin with a duck.

What a spin does in a phrase is carry momentum from one exchange into the next. A run of attacks ends, and a Saberist who simply stops has to start again from nothing; a Saberist who spins out of it arrives at the next beat already moving. That is what "flow" means here, and it is why the spins are placed exactly where the choreography changes character — after the parry run, before the lock, out of the lock, and into the finish. The opposing spins at step 8 do more: two Saberists turning away from each other at the same instant reset the whole geometry of the fight in one beat, and both come out of it facing a new exchange.

Holds are the other half, and they are the opposite instruction. Steps 9 and 10 chain them: a 9 parry in an inverted grip that binds, held across the step boundary with x, and closed into a second lock on the 12 line. Two locks joined by a carried bind, written in both rows — that is a long time to be bound, and it is what the run of spins has been building toward. Where the spins keep the movement travelling, the holds stop it dead and make the audience wait.

Then comes the passage that makes CM-T unusual. Steps 11 to 15 are the same in both rows, five beats in a row: both Saberists step forward, both step back and pause, both flourish overhead, both bash on the 4 line, both spin counter clockwise. Nobody attacks anybody. For five steps the two Saberists are not fighting — they are performing the same phrase at the same time, as a mirror.

That is a deliberate and slightly startling thing to write into a duel, and it does two jobs. In performance it reads as a reset: two opponents who have just spent ten steps bound together break apart, take stock, and circle. In training it is the hardest kind of synchronisation there is, because there is no attack to cue from. In an exchange, the parry has the attack to answer; in a mirror, both Saberists have only the count and each other. A pair that can hold five unison beats can hold anything else in the library.

The pause inside step 12 is worth its own attention. St-B (pause) writes a stop into the middle of a footwork step, which means the notation is specifying not just where to go but how long to be still on arrival. Between the flourish and the bash, that stillness is what makes the flourish land.

After the mirror, CM-T returns to ordinary business — 1, 8, 4, 10 answered by four parries, the plainest run in the movement — and then finishes on a hold. Saberist B carries a 2© and then a 12©, Saberist A ducks into a spin, blends the 3 line, and ends 1H (hold at bay): one hand on the saber, the other Saberist held off at the point of it. A movement built on flow ends by refusing to move at all.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-T is designed to teach:

  • spins as the connection between exchanges rather than as decoration
  • spinning both directions, and spinning opposite to a partner at the same beat
  • carrying a lock into the next move with x, and chaining two locks together
  • parries taken behind the back and in the inverted grip
  • unison passages where both Saberists perform identical cells
  • an overhead flourish performed by two people at once
  • a written pause inside a footwork step
  • ending a movement on a held position rather than a strike

docs.title: Phase 1: The spins alone
docs.text:
Both Saberists practise S CW and S CCW with no partner and no sequence.

Turn in each direction, slowly, and finish each spin facing a chosen point with the saber under control. Then practise the two turning at once in opposite directions, at walking pace, at a distance neither blade can cross. Spinning while a partner spins the other way is the beat most likely to surprise a pair at speed.

docs.title: Phase 2: The parry run
docs.text:
Walk steps 2 to 5 one at a time, with a full stop after each.

3, 9, 3, 9X against 3P, 9P, 3P, 9P is the simplest material in the movement and the foundation for everything after it. Confirm at every step that both Saberists agree which target the number names, that the parry meets the attack cleanly, and that the step can be repeated the same way.

docs.title: Phase 3: The awkward parries
docs.text:
Practise 3P (behind) and 9P IgX on their own.

One is taken behind the back and one in the inverted grip, and neither is a position a Saberist can improvise safely. Set each of them statically, without a partner first, then against a slow attack, and only then in sequence.

docs.title: Phase 4: The chained lock
docs.text:
Practise steps 9 and 10 as a single held block.

The bind enters on the 9 line in an inverted grip, is carried across the step boundary, and closes on the 12 line. Enter it slowly and by agreement, hold each stage for a full count, and treat the two locks as one continuous action rather than two separate ones.

docs.title: Phase 5: The unison passage
docs.text:
Rehearse steps 11 to 15 as a mirror, counted out loud.

This is the phase to spend the most time on. There is no attack to cue from, so the pair needs a shared count: step forward together, step back and hold the pause together, flourish together, bash together, spin together. Set the bash and the flourish for distance first — both blades are overhead at the same moment at step 13 — and then work purely on arriving at the same instant.

docs.title: Phase 6: The run and the finish
docs.text:
Walk steps 16 to 22 one at a time.

Four attacks, four parries, then the duck into a spin, the blend and the hold. Decide how long 1H (hold at bay) is held before it is ever performed in sequence — a hold that is not agreed will always be cut short by the Saberist who is less comfortable.

docs.title: Phase 7: Continuous flow, then pace
docs.text:
Run each part end to end at low speed, join all twenty-two steps, and only then add speed.

Speed belongs to the parry run and the attack run. It does not belong to the spins, the locks, the unison passage or the final hold. CM-T reads as flow only when the still beats are held at full length — a movement that rushes its pauses has no flow at all, only hurry.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-T should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

Three hazards belong to this movement. The first is the pair of opposing spins at step 8, where both Saberists turn at once and each loses sight of the other partway round — the distance for that beat is set at the widest point either blade reaches, not at the point they start from. The second is step 13, where both Saberists perform an overhead flourish simultaneously; two blades above two heads at the same moment is a beat to set slowly, with the distance agreed and checked every session. The third is step 14's 4B, a bash written identically in both rows, which means neither Saberist is defending and the blades meet because both aimed them there.

The chained lock deserves a mention of its own. A bind carried across a step boundary and closed into a second lock keeps two Saberists connected for longer than anywhere else in the library, and long binds invite small adjustments — a shift of grip, a lean, a step. Agree what the bind looks like at each stage and hold it there.

It is also worth naming what this movement adds to the notation. Nothing. Spins, footwork, flourishes, pauses and holds were all in the language already, and CM-T simply writes a movement in which they carry the weight and the attacks fill the gaps. A row of parries and a row of attacks is one kind of choreography. Two Saberists stepping, flourishing and turning in unison for five beats is another, and the same notation records both without a special case.

When CM-T is clean, continue to CM-U, or return to the Extended Library.

docs.title: CM-V
docs.text:
CM-V interprets the duel between Darth Vader and Obi-Wan Kenobi from the third episode of Kenobi.

It is twenty-seven steps of one-sided pressure. Saberist A attacks almost without pause; Saberist B answers six of those attacks by parrying and then shoving the attacker away, and never once takes the initiative. What the movement trains is what to do when you cannot win an exchange and can only survive it.

CM-V was notated by Stephen Carter.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
CM-V is written in three tables, numbered continuously through all twenty-seven steps.

Wide tables

The tables below are wide. On a phone, turn the device landscape; any of them can also be scrolled sideways.

The opening

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 s9 s10 Saberist A 9B 0 10© 3B Pause 9 Pause 5 9 Pause Saberist B 9P + Pushback St-B+L D 3P + Pushback 9P 5P 9P + Pushback

The middle

Player s11 s12 s13 s14 s15 s16 s17 s18 s19 s20 Saberist A 9 5 9x 9B Pause 12 9 7Px Saberist B 9P + Pushback S CCW 5P 9Px 9P + Pushback 11P 9P + Pushback S CW 7x

The finish

Player s21 s22 s23 s24 s25 s26 s27 Saberist A 11x SS > CCW x12 Pause 12x Guide x12 > x9 Force Push Saberist B 11Px SS > CW 11P 11Px Guide x11P > x9P

Read down each column as usual. Two words repeat more than any target number does: Pushback in Saberist B's row and Pause in Saberist A's.

  • Six of Saberist B's cells end in Pushback. Each is a parry and then a shove — 9P + Pushback five times and 3P + Pushback once — and each is answered on the following beat by a Pause or by Saberist A resetting to attack again.
  • Five of Saberist A's cells are Pause, and Saberist B has none. The attacking Saberist is the one who stops, every time, and it is always immediately after being pushed away or after a bash.
  • The 9 line carries the movement. Saberist A attacks it seven times across the twenty-seven steps. No other line appears more than twice.
  • B is a bash, 0 is a thrust as in CM-D, and © is a complete, taught in CM-C. All three appear in the first four steps, before the movement settles into its pattern.
  • x keeps a lock into the next move, from the Notation Legend. The last third of the movement is almost entirely bound: 9x against 9Px, 7Px against 7x, 11x against 11Px, then x12, 12x and 11Px again.
  • SS is the saber stand-off, the prolonged lock taught in CM-G and written S+S in the Legend. At step 22 both Saberists turn inside it, and their cells name opposite directions — SS > CCW against SS > CW. The demonstration video shows the turn.
  • Guide is written in both rows at step 26, where Saberist A's cell reads Guide x12 > x9: a bound blade moved from the 12 line to the 9 line while the bind is kept, with Saberist B guided along with it and answering x11P > x9P at the finish.
  • St-B+L is footwork — step back and left, from the Legend's St-B and St-L — and D is a duck. They are Saberist B's only two answers in the movement that are neither a parry nor a lock.
  • Force Push closes the movement, written for Saberist A alone.
  • A blank cell means nothing is written for that Saberist on that beat.

docs.title: Pushing back
docs.text:
Defence in the Core Library is a parry. The attack arrives, the blade meets it, and the exchange either changes hands — as CM-D sets out — or continues. Nothing in that arrangement addresses the situation CM-V is about, which is being attacked by someone you cannot answer.

Look at Saberist B's row across the whole movement. There is not one attack in it. Twenty-seven steps, and every cell is a parry, a lock, a step, a duck, a spin, or a shove. That much is shared with CM-L, which is also a defence with no counter in it. What CM-V adds is the shove.

9P + Pushback is a parry with something on the end of it. The blade meets the attack, and then Saberist B drives the attacker away — not to gain an opening, because Saberist B never takes one, but simply to make room. It happens six times, and the pattern around it is always the same: the parry stops the attack, the pushback buys distance, and Saberist A's next cell is a Pause or a fresh approach.

That is what makes the movement read the way it does. A defender who only parries looks overwhelmed. A defender who parries and shoves looks like someone holding a losing position on purpose, which is a different thing and a much harder thing to perform. The pushback is the difference between surviving and being beaten slowly, and it is written into the notation rather than left to acting.

Saberist A's pauses are the other half of the same idea. Five times the attacking Saberist simply stops — after the opening flurry, after a bash, after being pushed away. An attacker who never pauses is a machine, and an audience stops believing the defender can survive. The pauses are where the attacking Saberist chooses to stop, and they are what make the pressure legible as pressure rather than as noise.

Then the movement changes character completely. From step 14 onward, almost every beat is bound. 9x against 9Px, 7Px against 7x, 11x against 11Px — the lower-case x carries each bind into the next step rather than releasing it, so what would elsewhere be a series of separate locks is one long engagement that keeps changing shape. Distance, which the pushbacks kept opening, closes and stays closed.

At the centre of that is the stand-off at step 22, and it is the moment the whole movement has been arranged around. Both Saberists turn inside the bind. Their cells name opposite directions — SS > CCW and SS > CW — so the two of them rotate as one thing, which is only possible because the bind before it was held rather than remade.

The last two steps are unlike anything else in the library. Guide x12 > x9 moves a bound blade from one line to another without letting go of it, with Guide written in Saberist B's row too, because a guided blade needs both Saberists working. And then Force Push, written for Saberist A alone, with Saberist B's blade travelling x11P > x9P as it lands.

That ending is worth understanding for what it says about the movement rather than for its effect. CM-V spends twenty-six steps establishing that Saberist B can hold this off — parrying everything, shoving the attacker back six times, never once giving ground for free. Then the fight ends with something no parry answers. The pushbacks worked until they did not, which is exactly the shape of the scene the movement comes from.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-V is designed to teach:

  • defending for a full movement without ever taking the initiative
  • the parry-and-shove, and using distance rather than a counterattack as the answer
  • pausing as an attacker, so that pressure reads as deliberate
  • carrying a bind across many consecutive steps with x
  • turning inside a stand-off, with each Saberist naming their own direction
  • guiding a bound blade from one line to another
  • sustaining a single-line attack — seven attacks on the 9 — without it going flat

docs.title: Phase 1: The parry and the shove
docs.text:
Practise 9P + Pushback on its own, statically, before any sequence.

This is the movement's foundation and it appears six times, so it deserves more repetitions than anything else here. Agree exactly where the hands go, how far Saberist A travels, and how hard the shove is — then keep all three fixed. The Saberist being pushed provides the movement; the shove does not throw anybody.

docs.title: Phase 2: The opening statically
docs.text:
Walk steps 1 to 10 one at a time, with a full stop after each.

Confirm at every step:

  • both Saberists agree which target the number names
  • the parry meets the attack cleanly before the shove begins
  • the pauses are held for an agreed count rather than passed through
  • distance is safe
  • the step can be repeated the same way

docs.title: Phase 3: The repeated 9
docs.text:
Run steps 11, 15 and 18 as a set, out of sequence.

Saberist A attacks the 9 line seven times in this movement, and each one has to look like a fresh attempt rather than a repetition. Work on approaching the same line from different distances and at different speeds. This is a performance problem, not a technical one, and it is the thing most likely to make CM-V dull.

docs.title: Phase 4: The bind
docs.text:
Practise 9x into 9Px, 7Px into 7x, and 11x into 11Px as a continuous run.

The skill is the join rather than the lock: each bind is carried into the next step rather than released and remade. Enter every one slowly and by agreement, and walk the whole run at a quarter speed until both Saberists know where the other's blade is throughout.

docs.title: Phase 5: The stand-off and the turn
docs.text:
Set step 22 on its own.

Both Saberists turn inside a held bind, each in the direction their own cell names. Settle the stand-off first, without turning at all, then add rotation a quarter turn at a time, stopping at each stage to check the blades are still bound and neither Saberist has had to reach. Check the floor around the pair before every repetition.

docs.title: Phase 6: The guide and the finish
docs.text:
Practise Guide x12 > x9 against Guide, then the last beat.

A guided blade moves because both Saberists move it, so agree the path, the speed and the end position. Then set the Force Push and Saberist B's answer as an agreed pair — what it is, how far Saberist B travels, and how they arrive — exactly as any special move is agreed in CM-E.

docs.title: Phase 7: The whole movement, then pace
docs.text:
Join all twenty-seven steps at low speed.

Speed goes into Saberist A's attacks and Saberist B's parries. It does not go into the shoves, the binds, the stand-off, the guide or the finish. If either Saberist loses the sequence, restart from the beginning of the table they are in.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-V should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

The hazard that belongs to this movement is the pushback, and it is a hazard precisely because it happens six times and starts to feel routine. Hands on a partner are agreed the way an attack is agreed — placement, distance, force — and they are re-agreed at the start of every session rather than assumed from the last one. A pushback that grows by a few inches each repetition is the normal way this goes wrong, and neither Saberist will notice it happening.

The long bind is the other thing to watch. From step 14 to the end, the two Saberists are close together with blades engaged for most of the movement, and closeness that lasts stops registering as closeness. Reset the distance deliberately between repetitions.

It is also worth telling students what a row without a single attack in it is doing here. CM-L wrote one for a Saberist who parries sixteen times. CM-V writes another, and adds a way for that Saberist to affect the fight without ever striking — by taking back distance. A movement can be entirely defensive and still have both Saberists acting on each other, and the notation says so plainly: Pushback is a cell like any other.

When CM-V is clean, continue to CM-W, or return to the Extended Library.

docs.title: CM-W
docs.text:
CM-W interprets Diana's training bout against Antiope in Wonder Woman.

It is the longest movement in the Extended Library at thirty-one steps, and the only one that puts unarmed strikes in among the blade work. A back kick, a front kick and a punch are written as cells, on their own beats, in the same rows as the attacks — because the fight it comes from is a training bout between two people who are not only using weapons.

CM-W was notated by Desso and Anna Faulkner of Gulf Coast Saber Training.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
CM-W is written in four tables, read in order. Each starts its own count, as the source lesson writes them.

Wide tables

The tables below are wide. On a phone, turn the device landscape; any of them can also be scrolled sideways.

Part 1

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 s9 s10 Saberist A 11© 3 Pull left 10©A 7©A 12X Pull right 2XP 10XP 3PX Saberist B Dodge 3PM6X Pull R Duck Jump 12PX Pull L 2© 10© 3X

Part 2

Player s1 s2 Saberist A Saberist B Spin L>R Back Kick

Part 3

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 s9 s10 Saberist A 12 1P 10© 7© 12 Deflect 1P 11P Saberist B 12P 1 Duck Jump 12P Punch Spin R>L 1 Spin L>R 11

Part 4

Player s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8 s9 Saberist A 1P Front Kick 9© Dodge Dodge Special X Special Saberist B Spin R>L 1 Special Ig 1 Ig 11 Ig 12

Read down each column as usual, and notice how many cells have no blade in them at all.

  • Three cells are unarmed strikes. Back Kick closes Part 2, Punch sits at step 6 of Part 3, and Front Kick at step 3 of Part 4. Each occupies a full step, and Punch is answered by Deflect rather than by a parry.
  • © is a complete and ©A is a complete across — carried wide, vertically across — both taught in CM-C and listed in the Notation Legend. Every one of them is answered by leaving the line: Dodge, Duck, Duck, Jump, Jump.
  • The high ones are ducked and the low ones jumped. 10©A and 10© are ducked; 7©A and 7© are jumped. The pairing holds every time it appears.
  • The stand-off is pulled apart twice, at steps 3 and 7 of Part 1 — Pull left against Pull R, then Pull right against Pull L, the two Saberists going opposite ways each time, as in CM-G.
  • X is a lock, from CM-E. 12X against 12PX and 3PX against 3X are written with the lock in both rows; 2XP and 10XP are Saberist A's answers to completes and are written as the source lesson writes them, with the video showing each.
  • 3PM6X is a modified parry into a lock — a parry on the 3 line with the tip pointing down at 6, the Legend's 3PM6, closed into a lock.
  • Ig is the inverted grip taught in CM-J. Saberist B takes the last three attacks of the movement in it — Ig 1, Ig 11, Ig 12 — and Saberist A answers the first two by dodging.
  • Spin L>R and Spin R>L are spins, and there are four, all in Saberist B's row. Two of them, in Part 3, sit on beats where nothing is written for Saberist A.
  • Special closes the movement, in the sense CM-E gives it, and it appears three times in Part 4 — once for Saberist B, then Special X and Special for Saberist A.
  • Part 2 is two beats for Saberist B alone. Nothing is written for Saberist A while the spin and the back kick are performed.
  • A blank cell means nothing is written for that Saberist on that beat.

docs.title: Hands and feet
docs.text:
Every movement in the library so far assumes the fight is the blade. Saberists carry sabers, the notation names target lines, and when a cell describes something else — a duck, a spin, a pose — it is describing how a Saberist got out of the way of a blade or set up the next one. CM-P ends on a kick. CM-R has a shove in it. CM-W goes further: it treats a punch as an attack.

Look at step 6 of Part 3. Saberist B's cell says Punch. Saberist A's says Deflect. That is an attack and an answer, written exactly the way 1 and 1P are written, on the same beat, in the same table — and neither of them involves a saber. The notation did not need a new symbol for it, and it did not need to explain itself. A punch is a thing one Saberist does to another on a numbered beat, which is all a cell has ever meant.

The two kicks work the same way. Back Kick ends Part 2, on a beat where Saberist A has nothing written, so the kick lands into space the choreography has already cleared. Front Kick is Saberist A's at step 3 of Part 4, on a beat where Saberist B has nothing written. Both are placed where the other Saberist is not answering, which is the safest possible way to put an unarmed strike into a sequence and is worth noticing as a piece of craft.

That choice reflects the fight the movement comes from. This is a training bout rather than a duel — two people testing each other, where being disarmed or knocked down is a lesson rather than an ending. A notation that could only write blade work would have to leave out half of it.

The blade work that surrounds all this is unusually one-directional at the start. Part 1 opens with Saberist A throwing a complete, an attack, and then two completes across — 11©, 3, then 10©A and 7©A — and Saberist B answers every one by leaving the line. Dodge, duck, jump. Nothing is parried until the lock at step 6. That is CM-F's lesson again, performed with a saber in hand against the widest swings in the library.

The choice of answer is not arbitrary, and CM-W is the clearest place in the library to see the rule. 10©A and 10© are high, and both are ducked. 7©A and 7© are low, and both are jumped. Every complete in the movement follows it. A Saberist who learns that pairing here will read it correctly everywhere else.

Then the movement turns over. Part 3 hands the attack back and forth — 12 against 12P, then 1 against 1P — and by Part 4 Saberist B is attacking in an inverted grip while Saberist A dodges: Ig 1, Ig 11, Ig 12. A movement that opened with Saberist A driving forward ends with Saberist A retreating from a reversed blade.

And it ends on special moves. Saberist B takes one at step 5 of Part 4, Saberist A answers the inverted-grip run with Special X and then Special. Three slots the notation names without filling, at the end of thirty-one steps, in a movement about two people finding out what the other can do. That is the right place for them.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
CM-W is designed to teach:

  • unarmed strikes — punches and kicks — as written, counted beats
  • placing an unarmed strike where the other Saberist is not answering
  • answering a complete by its height: ducking the high ones, jumping the low ones
  • completes across, and the distance they need
  • pulling apart from a stand-off, twice, in both directions
  • attacking in an inverted grip against a retreating partner
  • holding a thirty-one step movement together across four tables

docs.title: Phase 1: Completes and their answers
docs.text:
Practise 11©, 10©A, 7©A, 10© and 7© with the dodges, ducks and jumps that answer them.

A complete across travels further than anything most Saberists have performed, and there are four completes in Part 1 alone. Set the height and arc of each, agree whether it is ducked or jumped, and rehearse each pair until both Saberists arrive together. None of this is run at speed early.

docs.title: Phase 2: Part 1 statically
docs.text:
Walk the ten steps of Part 1 one at a time, with a full stop after each.

Confirm at every step:

  • both Saberists agree which target the number names
  • the evasion leaves the line the swing is travelling on
  • the lock is entered with control rather than collided into
  • distance is safe for a swing that does not stop
  • the step can be repeated the same way

docs.title: Phase 3: The stand-offs and the pulls
docs.text:
Practise 12X into the pull, and the second pull at step 7, as units.

Enter each bind slowly and by agreement, then break it by pulling in opposite directions on an agreed count. Neither Saberist is trying to win the bind. Set the direction, the count and the distance each travels, and keep them fixed.

docs.title: Phase 4: The unarmed strikes
docs.text:
Rehearse Back Kick, Punch against Deflect, and Front Kick, each on its own.

These are the beats that need the most agreement and the least speed. For each: agree the target, agree the distance, make no contact, and perform it the same way every repetition. Two of the three land on beats where the other Saberist has nothing written, and that spacing is part of the safety — it is not an invitation to move into the gap.

docs.title: Phase 5: Part 3 and the spins
docs.text:
Run Part 3 as a sequence, then work Saberist B's two spins separately.

The spins at steps 7 and 9 fall on beats where nothing is written for Saberist A, so Saberist B is turning while the other Saberist holds. Agree the direction and the spacing before either is run in sequence.

docs.title: Phase 6: The inverted-grip run
docs.text:
Practise Ig 1, Ig 11 and Ig 12 against the two dodges.

Saberist B takes the grip before the run rather than during it, as CM-J sets out, and works all three attacks statically first. Saberist A is dodging rather than parrying for two of the three, so the distance is set from Saberist A's side.

docs.title: Phase 7: The specials, then the whole movement
docs.text:
Decide all three special moves before they are practised, then join the four tables at low speed.

Do not improvise the specials during practice. When the whole movement runs, add speed only to the exchanges in Parts 1 and 3 — never to the completes across, the locks, the pulls, the unarmed strikes or the specials.

docs.title: Teaching note
docs.text:
CM-W should be taught as a language drill, not as a fight.

Two hazards belong to this movement. The first is the unarmed strikes. A punch and two kicks are the only attacks in the library delivered with a part of the body rather than a blade, and the instinct that keeps a saber at a safe distance does not automatically transfer to a fist or a foot. All three are performed with no contact, at an agreed distance, at a speed that never increases — and the beats around them, where the other Saberist has nothing written, stay empty.

The second is length. Thirty-one steps across four tables is the longest thing in the Extended Library, and the honest way to work it is one table at a time across several sessions. Part 2 is two beats long and easy to lose entirely; it is a real part of the count, and skipping it puts the pair out of step for the whole of Part 3.

It is also worth telling students what this movement settles about the notation. A punch answered by a deflect is written the same way as a 1 answered by a 1P — same table, same beat, same two rows. Nothing had to be added to the system to hold it. The Saber Standard describes what two Saberists do to each other in sequence, and a saber is one of the things they might be holding while they do it.

CM-W is the last movement in the Extended Library. When it is clean, the whole of that library is behind you — browse the Community Library for movements contributed by other schools, or return to the Extended Library.

docs.title: Community Library
docs.text:
The Community Library holds movements developed and contributed by Saberists, schools, and clubs outside the founding Core and Extended libraries. Community movements are credited to their contributing school or individual. Over time, a movement here may be promoted into the Extended or Core libraries.

No movements have been submitted to the Community Library yet.

docs.title: Contributing a movement
docs.text:
If your school or club has built its own CM and wants to share it with the wider SaberCraft community, see Contribute for how submissions work.

Schools building their own internal CM libraries first — without submitting to the shared standard — can also see For Schools and the worked example below.

docs.title: Creating your own system
docs.text:
Build and customize your own system using your school's program, then share it with the community.

Any theatre or saber choreography club work can be converted into a library you can use to structure your classes. The same library can serve as your school's own collection of staged choreography battles, and the same approach can be used to create your own LUMINA Battles if you want to introduce game play.

To get started, use the Create Your Own CMs worksheet.

The choreography is not the standard; the notation language is. That distinction is what lets schools collaborate without becoming identical. You keep your own movement library, naming structure, ranking system, and teaching style, and still write it all in a notation any other school can read.

docs.title: A worked example: NY Kendo School
docs.text:
"NY Kendo School" is a fictional school, used here to show how an independent group documents original movement in Saber Standard Notation. It names its movements KS-A, KS-B, KS-C under its own prefix rather than using SaberCraft's CM codes, and the notation stays readable either way.

Its first sequence, KS-A "Crosswind Exchange":

Player Step 1 Step 2 Step 3 Step 4 Step 5 Step 6 Saberist A 11 1 9 3 7 5 Saberist B 11P 1P 9P 3P 7P 5P

The sequence demonstrates:

  • a fixed attacker and defender across the whole exchange
  • a direct attack-to-parry pairing on every step
  • the three opposite target-line pairs taken in turn: 11 and 1, then 9 and 3, then 7 and 5

Saberist A holds the attacking role for all six steps while Saberist B answers each line, which keeps the pattern readable at slow speed. The point is not the choreography itself but the interoperability: a SaberCraft instructor could read this sequence, and an NY Kendo School instructor could read a SaberCraft CM.

docs.title: A shared ecosystem
docs.text:
In a larger choreography ecosystem, schools might publish side by side:

School Example library SaberCraft CM-A through CM-X NY Kendo School KS-A through KS-T Performance Team Stage Exchanges

Each library remains unique. The notation provides the common structure that makes choreography readable across communities.

docs.title: Core Library
docs.text:
The Core Library is the official beginner foundation of the Saber Standard: CM-A through CM-E. Every Saberist starts here. These five movements establish targeting, attack/parry pairing, role-switching, flow, and the basic vocabulary that every later movement — Extended or Community — builds on.

Work down the table in order. CM-C is taught in two parts: its completes must be understood before the full sequence can be performed.

CM-D is the threshold in this sequence, not simply the next item. Through CM-A to CM-C one Saberist attacks and the other defends from start to finish, so a student reads one active row and one answering it. From CM-D the attack changes hands mid-sequence and both rows are active — the point at which the notation starts describing a dialogue rather than a run of attacks. Expect it to take longer than the movements before it.

docs.title: LUMINA Games
docs.text:
Completely optional

LUMINA Games are an add-on, not a requirement. Any organization using the Saber Standard is free to adopt them as a way to expand what it offers, and equally free to leave them aside. Adopting the notation does not commit a school, club, or Saberist to competitive play.

docs.title: LUMINA: saber battles remixed
docs.text:
LUMINA is a weapon combat-based sport where Lumens (players) compete for points in timed rounds using choreographed movement sequences (CMs). It is part choreography and part improvisation, built to develop saber mastery among its participants.

All attacks are communicated before an exchange using a telegraph: a silent gesture the attacker performs to specify which CM they will deliver.

LUMINA is built around teamwork. Teams of Lumens work together to create the most compelling fight choreography and to out-perform the other teams. In each match, Lumens are paired with other players to battle in choreographed combat, and each player gains points every time they successfully commit or defend a sequence. The objective is to collect the highest number of points.

Duets games usually end with a pair of winners. Players who compete across multiple games in a season accumulate points across those games, and the Lumen with the highest total wins the season.

docs.title: How to train for LUMINA
docs.text:
LUMINA combines CMs that you and your partner already know, so players from beginner through advanced can take part.

Before playing, work through the following:

  1. Learn the notation. Start with the Notation Overview.
  2. Learn as many CMs as you like. The more CMs you know, the more interesting the matches become.
  3. Learn the telegraph for each CM you plan to use.
  4. Learn the rules of LUMINA.

Suggested CM knowledge by level:

Level Should know Beginner CM-A, CM-B, CM-C, CM-D Intermediate CM-A through CM-J Advanced CM-A through CM-M and beyond

The LUMINA rulebook is listed on the Downloads page.

docs.title: How to score points
docs.text:
Each CM is worth points according to its tier.

Tier Points CMs Simple +1 CM-A, CM-H, CM-Q Advanced +2 CM-B, CM-C, CM-G, CM-I, CM-J, CM-N, CM-Q, CM-R, CM 11, CM 12, CM 13 Extended +3 CM-D, CM-E, CM-F, CM-L, CM-O, CM-R, CM-S, CM 12, CM 14 Super +4 CM-K, CM-O, CM-P

docs.title: Power Plays
docs.text:
CMs can be played in combination, producing a Power Play worth an additional point.

The attacker must combine two different telegraphs before engaging in the attack. A maximum of two CMs can be played consecutively. Power Play points are granted to the team as part of each of their individual scores, and the total depends on the complexity of the CMs used.

Combination Power Play bonus Total points 2 Simple CMs +1 3 1 Simple + 1 Advanced +1 4 2 Advanced CMs +1 5 1 Advanced + 1 Extended +1 6 2 consecutive Extended forms +1 7 1 Super + 1 Extended +1 8

For example, CM-A (worth 1 point) plus CM-H (worth 1 point), plus 1 for the Power Play, results in 3 points for that turn.

docs.title: Round types
docs.text: LUMINA is played in two game types.

docs.title: Against the Clock (Speed)
docs.text:
1. Gather several participants.
  2. Split them into teams of two Lumens each.
  3. Select a time-based match, for example two minutes with unlimited rounds.
  4. Roll a die or flip a coin to determine the opening team. The highest roll opens the game, or the teams can agree an order.
  5. Flip a coin for the opening attacker, or use another selection method.
  6. Begin the timer.
  7. Lumen A telegraphs a CM of choice to Lumen B.
  8. Both engage in the turn.
  9. On successful completion, the roles switch.
  10. Lumen B telegraphs a CM of choice to Lumen A.
  11. Both engage in the turn.
  12. On successful completion, the turn is over and roles switch.
  13. When the second turn finishes, the round is over. Continue to the next round.
  14. Repeat until the timer runs out.
  15. Determine points based on the CMs and Power Play combinations.
  16. The team that rolled the next highest number goes next.

docs.title: Set Rounds
docs.text:
1. Gather several participants.
  2. Split them into teams of two Lumens each.
  3. Select a round-based match, for example three rounds where each player takes three turns, for a total of six exchanges, up to a three minute maximum.
  4. Roll a die or flip a coin to determine the opening team. The highest roll opens the game, or the teams can agree an order.
  5. Flip a coin for the opening attacker, or use another selection method.
  6. Begin the timer for the entire match.
  7. Lumen A telegraphs a CM of choice to Lumen B.
  8. Both engage in the turn.
  9. On successful completion, the roles switch.
  10. Lumen B telegraphs a CM of choice to Lumen A.
  11. Both engage in the turn.
  12. On successful completion, the turn is over and roles switch.
  13. When the second turn finishes, the round is over. Continue to the next round.
  14. Repeat until the timer runs out or the designated end round is complete.
  15. Determine points based on the CMs and Power Play combinations.
  16. The team that rolled the next highest number goes next.

docs.title: Winning a game
docs.text:
The winning team is the one that achieves the most points in a given match.

Games usually end with four winners: two for Speed and two for Rounds. Tournaments may be played in brackets, as singles or doubles.

docs.title: Judging
docs.text: Players present How to judge Only two Record the match on a camera or phone and make the calls afterwards Three or more Have at least one player watch and make the calls

docs.title: Winning the season
docs.text:
A season is conducted across three games. Each game day has a Speed division and a Rounds division.

To win the season, a Lumen must have the highest score across the whole season, adding their scores across all three games within a division. Keep the Speed and Rounds division scores separate.

For example, a player competing in Speed across all three games scores 30, 25, and 25. Their seasonal score is 80.

The player with the highest total is the champion for the season, with second and third place following. If there is a tie for any place, a tie-breaker decides it, and the loser of the tie-breaker takes the lower place.

docs.title: Teams and incomplete CMs
docs.text:
Teams are two Lumens working together. The objective is for you and your teammate to complete as many CMs as you can.

If the attacker strikes the wrong target point or hesitates, or if the defender does not defend properly against a CM attack, the CM is incomplete.

Either Lumen may go first, and there are several ways to choose. Once a player has been designated to begin the match, they perform their CM. When they are done, their teammate takes a turn and chooses their own CM. Once that is complete, the round is over. Players keep switching back and forth, and each player should have a turn in every round.

Two examples:

  • Lumen 1 telegraphs CM-B. Lumen 2 acknowledges. Lumen 1 performs all the moves of CM-B, Lumen 2 successfully blocks every strike, the CM is successful, and the team scores.
  • Lumen 1 telegraphs CM-B. Lumen 2 acknowledges. Lumen 1 begins CM-B and, as they approach, Lumen 2 hesitates and locks up. Lumen 1 stops, as there is no block in place, and their turn is over. It is now Lumen 2's turn.

docs.title: Language and terminology
docs.text: Term Meaning Saberist A practitioner of the Saber Standard, its notation, or its games Lumen A player Duet A team of Lumens working together in a match Telegraph A silent gesture the attacker performs to specify which CM or Power Play they will deliver Power Play A combination of two CMs performed successfully and consecutively Turn One exchange where a participant completes their exchange. In a two-person game the turn ends after one player has completed one exchange, then their opponent's turn begins Round Two turns. A round completes when each Lumen has taken one turn Match A series of rounds between two Lumens Game A collection of matches of the same type, either Against the Clock or Set Rounds Set Rounds A game type completed when a series of rounds between two Lumens has finished Against the Clock A game type where an unlimited series of turns is played within a set time. The standard match is two minutes per Duet Win A count of points granted to a player or team for successfully completing a match Draw An equal number of points granted to the players of a game Loss A count of points given to the player who scores fewer points in a match Ranking Overall standing, taking all players into account Incomplete A turn interrupted by the attacker or defender missing a particular movement in a CM

docs.title: Advanced Rules
docs.text:
These rules extend the base LUMINA Games format with the structures used on a full game day: how players are arranged, how a failing sequence can be recovered, how the Baseline and handicaps work, and the quick reference used during play.

For the core format, scoring values, and Power Play combinations, start with the Games overview.

docs.title: Arranging players for game day
docs.text:
Game days are usually split into two game types: Against the Clock and Rounds-based. Lumens competing are expected to enroll in one or both.

When you join a game type, you play twice, in two match types: once with a partner you choose, and once with a partner drawn at random.

For example, in Game 1:

  • Against the Clock. Wilhelm chooses to play his first match with Valerie. The judges draw randomly from all players and pair Wilhelm with another Lumen at the game, Sarah. Wilhelm and Valerie finish their match with 25 points. Wilhelm plays again with Sarah and scores 20 points. Wilhelm keeps the higher of the two as his Speed score for Game 1: 25.
  • Rounds-based. Wilhelm again chooses Valerie for his first match. The judges pair him randomly with Charly. Wilhelm and Valerie finish with 23 points. Wilhelm plays again with Charly and scores 30 points. Wilhelm keeps the higher of the two as his Rounds score for Game 1: 30.

We suggest running the day in this order, from easiest to most difficult:

  1. Rounds — Chosen
  2. Rounds — Random
  3. Speed — Chosen
  4. Speed — Random

Lumens are given the Random match type in both game types so they have a chance at an even better score by leaning on improvisation. In Chosen battles, partners have time to strategize; in Random ones they do not. This is where LUMINA combines what a Lumen knows of choreography with how they apply it under pressure.

A Lumen should battle once with their choice of partner for each game type, and may not play more than once for the same game type and match type.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
Recovery is the act of saving a failing CM during the exchange.

If a partner loses their place or becomes confused, and their partner can get them back on track in fewer than two moves, the CM is recovered and counts for its full points, including Power Plays.

Getting a Duet back on track comes down to pace. Both partners should work together to pick up a possibly incomplete CM or Power Play by holding a consistent pace throughout that does not deviate. Three or more misses in a CM constitutes an Incomplete.

Example recoveries:

  • The Lumens end up switching offensive and defensive roles, but both make the switch at the same time and complete the sequence on the opposite side. Assuming the pace stays consistent, this counts as a recovery.
  • The Lumens switch roles mid-CM, but again both make the switch at the same time and complete the sequence. Assuming the pace stays consistent, this counts as a recovery.

docs.title: The Baseline
docs.text:
The champion plays a coaching role and becomes a judge in the following season. That role is titled the Baseline.

The Baseline's score is not tallied, but they may partner with active Lumens who are competing, giving those players the advantage of their proficiency. The Baseline fills empty spots in any game where an odd number of players is available. Their partner receives the points from the round; the Baseline does not.

If a Baseline opts not to judge 75% or more of the following season's matches, they are disqualified from participating in that season's games.

docs.title: Handicaps
docs.text:
A handicap offers an advantage or disadvantage to players. In any given game, a set of CMs may be worth more or fewer points than usual. This can shake things up, so that a CM normally worth many points may be worth less for one game.

For example, judges may agree that CM-N and CM-G are worth 5 points for an upcoming game, while CM-D and CM-E are worth 1 point. This encourages Lumens to learn as many CMs as possible so they are ready when handicaps come into play.

Handicaps should be communicated at least two weeks before the next game, and they apply to both formats.

docs.title: Adjudication awards
docs.text:
At the end of the season, the following awards are given.

Award Criteria 1st place The Lumen with the most points across the entire season 2nd place The Lumen with the second most points across the entire season 3rd place The Lumen with the third most points across the entire season Vanguard The Lumen with the highest average number of wins, having competed in at least half the games

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
Seek the advice of a physician before starting any exercise routine.

As in any sport, injuries can occur, and safety gear is always recommended, including padded gloves, eye protection, and proper athletic wear.

docs.title: Pocket quick reference
docs.text:
The arena

  • Play must be conducted in a designated area or arena. A minimum of 30' × 30' is recommended.
  • Players are discouraged from playing out of bounds. If players enter an out-of-bounds area, the turn is interrupted and they must return to the arena. If play continues out of bounds rather than returning, points for that turn are nullified and the Duet returns to the centre of the arena, with the defender beginning the next turn. The clock continues throughout.

Matches and rounds

  • Matches and recoveries should be non-verbal. Lumens should not talk while playing.
  • Each match is set either by time limit or by a predesignated number of rounds, based on the game type.
  • Each round consists of turns between Lumens. Against the Clock has unlimited rounds; Rounds-based runs up to three rounds.
  • A turn is where one participant engages the other using either one CM, or up to two CMs in a Power Play.
  • Participants switch the attacker role after each turn.
  • If the timer runs out mid-exchange, that turn does not count. If both Lumens were in the middle of a Power Play, it is invalidated no matter how far they got.

Play

  • The attacker must telegraph the incoming CM or Power Play to the defender.
  • Attackers must step forward. Defenders must step backward.
  • Styled pauses and locks also count as steps.
  • Lumens may pass a CM or Power Play by telegraph. Their teammate continues to offer telegraphs until the Lumen nods to engage.
  • If the attacker forgets a strike, the CM is invalid and the turn switches to the defender, unless the team delivers a successful Recovery.
  • Lumens may stop the match at any time by making the pass gesture at the judges and lowering their weapon.

Points

  • CMs carry preassigned point values by category: Simple 1, Advanced 2, Extended 3, Super 4.
  • The team is awarded points if attacker and defender successfully complete a CM.
  • Points are awarded to the team, not to individual players.
  • A +10 bonus is awarded for a match in which no CMs are repeated. Every CM in that match must be unique across both Lumens, so once one Lumen plays CM-B, neither may use it again.
  • A striking participant incurs a penalty if their partner is injured. The worse the injury, the worse the penalty: a minimum of 1 point, up to disqualification.

Pairing

Lumens should be paired to succeed as well as they can. When selecting a chosen or random partner, options may be limited. If a Lumen wishes to play but knows only a few CMs, and other players do not want to team with them because it would limit their own seasonal scores, there are options:

  • That Lumen may work with the Baseline, so more advanced players are unaffected.
  • That Lumen may work with a more advanced Lumen, chosen or random, where the more advanced player forfeits their individual score and acts as the Baseline. The advanced Lumen keeps the score from their other match.

docs.title: Running two versions
docs.text:
In larger groups it helps to run two versions of the game, depending on player level.

Version Who it is for How it runs Fundamentals Beginners Uses a small number of CMs, with more lenient strike and defence rules Advanced Experienced Lumens Opens up more or all of the CMs, with rules strictly enforced

docs.text:
